Hon. W. T. WHITE (Minister of Finance) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 110, to amend the Insurance Act, 1910.
He said: The amendments proposed are designed to meet certain defects in the

existing Insurance Act, and particularly those which have been revealed by the recent liquidation and inquiry by the liquidator into the affairs of the Union Life Insurance Company.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I notice that the resolution is not yet moved.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I may explain that there are two Bills. The one to which the resolution refers is that relating to Civil Service insurance. But the present Bill requires no resolution as it involves no expenditure by the Government. The principal provisions of this Bill are as follows: Greater powers are given the department to deal with insolvent life insurance companies. The amendments in this regard are designed to meet certain defects in the existing Act and in the Winding-up Act relating to life insurance companies. There is also provision to the effect that in the case of contracts entered into between life insurance companies and any of their directors, officers or agents, in the event of liquidation, the liquidator may elect either to continue such contracts or to terminate them, no matter for what time they may have been originally entered into; and, in the event of the liquidator electing to terminate them, the holder of the contract shall be entitled to rank for only three months' time of the contract. This is to meet a difficulty that arose in connection with the Union Life Insurance Company, which I will explain at greater length on the second reading of the Bill. The legal result of the contract in that case was that a very large sum indeed-on account of the length of the contract-would have been payable by the insurance company in respect of damages which would, of course, rank upon the assets of the company pari passu with the claims of the policy holders. There is a further provision of importance, that, in the event of liquidation, the claims of the policy-holders shall he a first charge upon the assets. I think these are the chief amendments relating to life insurance companies which are insolvent or are in liquidation.
In addition, there are certain amendments under which companies are not permitted to invest in the shares of other companies carrying on the same class of business. Companies now holding such shares are required to dispose of their holdings within a certain time. Ten years is the time specified.
There are more stringent provisions as to
the supervison of companies in process or organization, particularly as to the expenses of such organization. A limitation is placed on investments in unsecured bonds in which companies are authorized to invest, and there is a provision whereby the liquidator of a life insurance company may, subject to certain conditions and with the consent of the court, re-insure the policyholders of the insolvent company. That is, of course, in the interest of the policyholders. There is also provision in the case of fire insurance companies that if there should he a twenty-five per cent impairment of the capital the superindentent of insurance may call upon the company to>
make good the deficiency.

I notice the hon. minister mentioned as one of the features of the Bill that in case of liquidation the policy is to be the first claim upon the assets of the company. Is that a departure from the present law?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am advised that it is; I think that the claims now rank pari passu upon the assets.
All claims?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My right hon. friend would hardly expect me to say offhand whether all claims are in that position. I believe they are. This is designed to meet a situation that arose in connection with the Union Life, in which all claims ranked equally with the claims of policy-holders, and to provide that the claims of policyholders shall have the first place.

Would my
hon. friend, on the next occasion when this Bill is before us, be in a position to tell us exactly the law on this point?
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speakeroldname: Mr. F. B. CARVELL (Carleton, N.B.) moved :
subtopic: THE CASE OF WILLIAM J. KELLY.
speechtext:
For a copy of all petitions, letters, affidavits, telegrams and documents to and by the Department of Justice, or any other department of Government, on behalf of or in reference to Wm. J. Kelly, a prisoner in the United States federal prison at Atlanta, Ga., and of all the letters, telegrams and other memoranda between the Department of Justice, or any other department of the Government, and the British Ambassador at Washington, or the Government of the United States, regarding the imprisonment and proposed liberation of the said Wm. J. Kelly.
He said: In moving for the production of these papers, I wish to draw the attention of the House to what, in my view, is one of the hardest cases that I have known for many years and which really has assumed an international aspect.
In, the month of April in the
4	p.m. year 1903, a man named William
J.	Kelly, a farmeT living within three or four miles of the boundary line, was drawing a load of potatoes from his home to the market on the American side of the line. He was doing what I am sorry to say is done by hundreds of people in that section of the country: he was drawing potatoes by night and not in the day time. I am not attempting in any way to

minimize or mitigate the offence. Between one and two o'clock on an April morning, Kelly was found about fifteen or twenty rods beyond the boundary line by a United States customs officer. He was ordered to throw up bis bands and to surrender his team and load. Kelly, however, did not feel disposed to do that. It is pretty hard	to	tell	what really	tookplace	on	that occasion. I	have
beard the matter detailed in court by both Kelly and Mr. Burns, the United States customs officer, on two occasions, one ;in the year 1903 and the other in the year 1910. They both tell practically the same story. The story brieflly is as follows: Kelly was riding on the top of a wagon containing fourteen or fifteen barrels of potatoes. The officer ordered him to halt, which I do not think he did. The officer then seized his horses' bridles, and, almost simultaneously with this act, Kelly jumped from his wagon and the officer fired at him with his revolver. The first shot took effect in Kelly's cheek, followed around under the skin and lodged in the back of the neck. The second shot struck a heavy belt buckle which Kelly was wearing around his waist; that deflected the bullet and the man's life was saved. By this time Kelly was on top of the officer with his sled stake. There is no doubt that Kelly handled the officer very roughly. I do not know that when he left the man he thought or cared very much whether he was dead or alive. The officer, however, was put out of action. Kelly then made his way back to his own side of the line and to his own home, although at that time he was suffering with a 32-calibre revolver bullet in his neck. Medical aid was summoned, the bullet was removed, and Kelly finally recovered.
Very shortly after that proceedings were taken by the United States authorities to have Kelly extradited ffor assaulting 'a customs officer in the discharge of his duties. At that time there were only a few crimes that were extraditable. The first was murder, the next manslaughter; and, of this particular class of crime, the next was assault with intent to commit murder. Therefore the United States authorities applied to have Kelly extradited on the ground that he had committed an assault on the officer Burns, with intent to commit murder. The matter was very fiercely contested. Eminent counsel were employed - by the United States authorities, and the case was tried before the late Mr. Justice Gregory, Justice of the Supreme Court. After a very extended hearing, Mr. Justice Gregory decided that Kelly's offence did not come within that clause of the Extradition Act, as he did not find that Kelly had assaulted the officer with intent to murder, but had assaulted the officer practically in self protection.
Of course, that did not alter the fact that Kelly was in violation of the customs laws of the United States. But, at that time, as I think to-day, an infraction of the customs laws either of the United States or of Canada was not an extraditable offence; therefore Kelly was liberated. He was a poor man with a farm worth probably $2,000 or $2,200. There was a small mortgage on it at'the time, and a larger mortgage was put on shortly after. He had a small amount of personal property and a family of ten or eleven children. He was barely eking out an existence. A subscription was taken up among his friends' to defray pan of the expenses, but only a small portion was defrayed. He went back to his home, and remained an honourable, law-abiding citizen for six years. It seems that about fourteen or fifteen years before this Kelly had been at Houlton, a town on the American side two or three miles from the border, and had been charged with smuggling and his team was seized. He got the team'out of the stable, and went home, considering that he had a perfect right to do so I do not think that this could have been regarded as a serious offence, because he had been back and forth to Houlton about as often as to his own market town, perhaps oftener, because up and down the boundary line, the boundary exists largely in name only so far as the ordinary small affairs of everyday life are concerned. He travelled back and forward unmolested. But it appears that an indictment had been preferred against him before the grand jury and a true Bill found. Just why, I do not know, but the fact is that the true Bill was allowed to stand, the proceedings were dropped, and nothing took place for four-teeen years-in fact, for twenty years.
Kelly received all the instruction which a counsel could give to a client-I happened to be his counsel, and I know what I am talking about-never again, as long as he lived, to set foot on American soil, because I believed that if he did the American *authorities would arrest him, and if he were arrested, having flagrantly violated their customs laws, and as their officer had been so severely handled, he would be punished to the full extent of the law. For the Am-

erican officer was severely handled. No bones were broken, but he was pounded with a stake until practically unconscious and left by the side of the road. Some one came along and took him to a neighbouring house. The extradition proceedings were on within a fortnight, and this officer, Burns, was able to come fifty miles from his home to Woodstock to give evidence. I am not trying, however, to minimize the fact that it was a pretty serious infraction of the customs laws of the United States.
Now, as I understand it, Kelly abode by the instruction of his counsel for six years. But then, relying, I am afraid, on fireside law, he seems to have believed that in that time the thing was outlawed, and so he went back; that is, it was claimed he went back, I do not know how truly. It is said that he was seen there in the summer of 1909. This angered the United States officials, and they started out to punish him. And here is where came in what I hold to be reprehensible conduct on their part and something for which our Government should call upon them to answer.
Just before the events in 1909 of which I have spoken, a man appeared at Kelly's farm representing himself to be a Mr. Black. Black wanted to buy poultry and almost anything else that a farmer had to sell for the Thanksgiving market in the United States. I may say that in that portion of New Brunswick ,a large business is carried on in raising poultry and disposing of it at very good prices. Black remained through that day and I think he came back the next day, and made a trade with Kelly to convey his purchases, consisting of poultry, a cow and a number of other items, to some point in American territory. Kelly said be only agreed to take them to the boundary line. But the American officers said he agreed to take them to Hodgdon, which by the way they travel, is three or four miles from Houlton. They went by what is called the lower road and struck the boundary line at Union Corner. For half a mile the highway is the international boundary line, the actual line being practically in the ditch on the American side. That is, the travelled roadway is on the Canadian side, though what you would call the three or four rods of the highway allowance is partly in American and partly Canadian territory. The maintenance and upkeep of that half mile of road is managed internationally in some way, and both parties do work upon it. There is no trouble to locate the boundary, because 
within the last four or five years the international boundary line has been very accurately delimited and marked out by granite posts set in concrete foundations. There is a post at Union Corner, another forty rods further north at the brow of a small hill, and another between a half and a third of a mile further north just where the road turns and goes into American territory. So, there is no difficulty in a person telling exactly where the American boundary line is. Kelly says that just before he reached the point at Crane's Corner where the road turns into American territory, he was set upon by a nUm-b'er of men who appeared in the darkness. Wherever it was, he was captured and taken to Houlton and put in jail. He was allowed during the night to telephone to some of his friends, and immediately he told his story. Of course, we have no way of proving what took place except by the evidence of Kelly and thte officers who were there. However, Kelly was entrapped and sent off to Portland and was tried there in the month of January following, I think, and was found guilty and sentenced to ten years, the full maximum penalty for assault upon a police officer,, and to four years for the old offence of twenty years before. And the sentences did not run concurrently, but the sentence for the old offence was to follow on the expiration of the first sentence of ten years.
I was present at the trial in Portland, as T was at the extradition proceedings, and I think we had the ablest counsel, probably, in that portion of the state of Maine at that time, ex-Judge Foster, formerly a judge of the Supreme Court of Maine, a man who had a long criminal experience. Mr. Foster, I am satisfied, did everything a man could do to acquit his client. And I am not prepared to say that Kelly did not receive a fair trial. The trial was conducted in as gentlemanly and proper manner as any one could wish. We tried to go into the evidence as to the manner in which Kelly was captured, but the judge held that once the prisoner was in United States territory the court had jurisdiction over the body. As a bald proposition of law, I must say I could not find very much fault with that position. However, try as hard as we would to introduce evidence as to the manner of his being captured, we were denied it, and the result was that the case went to the jury purely upon the question of whether or not he assaulted the officer.

subtopic: THE CASE OF WILLIAM J. KELLY.
speechtext: Was an attempt made to rely on the ground that he had really been arrested in Canada?

subtopic: THE CASE OF WILLIAM J. KELLY.
speechtext:
Yes. I was given the
right to act as counsel, to examine and cross-examine and re-examine, and I attempted to draw out that part of it, but the court, very courteously but equally firmly, refused to allow me to go into it, contending that once he was within American territory, no matter by what means, they had jurisdiction over the body, that they were trying him for an offence admittedly committed ' in American territory six years before and therefore the whole question of fact for that jury at that time was: Did he assault Burns six years previously or not. I think my right hon. friend will find that the American authorities at least would have authorities for that proposition in law. However, they so-held, and any and all evidence showing the manner in which the man had been inveigled into American territory was excluded. Therefore the only evidence that went before that jury was the question of fact:	Did Kelly
assault Officer Burns six year before or not. We attempted to. set up the defence that while he was guilty of smuggling they could not deny that his attack on Burns was purely a matter of self-preservation and selfdefence. After having listened to the* evidence of these two men on two separate occasions, after making all due allowance for the fact that he was my client and my friend, that he was a Canadian and that we were in foreign territory, yet I did come to the conclusion that Kelly was acting in self-defence. I did believe and I do now believe that Officer Burns fired on him long before there was any necessity of taking such drastic action. A man could not run away very fast with a team of horses, up a hill with an eight or ten per cent grade, when the officer was at the horses heads, as he admitted. I never could see why it was necessary to fire on the man as he did.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: THE CASE OF WILLIAM J. KELLY.
speechtext: Was the officer who arrested Kelly the second time and who fired on him, tue same man whom he had assaulted six years before?

subtopic: THE CASE OF WILLIAM J. KELLY.
speechtext:
Oh, no. I have an affidavit here, which I shall read in a short time, giving Kelly's side of the case. The jury brought in a verdict of guilty and the sentence was suspended until a later day in term. A proposition was then made to Judge Foster and myself, asking us if we would plead guilty to the old indictment. After considerable consultation with the
prisoner and with the prosecuting attorney, who is called the county attorney, we agreed that Kelly was to plead guilty with a distinct understanding that extreme leniency would be shown him. I can only say that they gave him four years for the old case. They may call that extreme leniency Because they might have given him ten years, but it did seem to me that the extremeness of the leniency was not as great as I had anticipated. The result was that the man was sent to Atlanta, Georgia and he is there to-day.
You may ask me wdiat took place and what right this Parliament or this Government would have to ask for the release of this prisoner. That is a very pertinent question, because the case I have given so far has not disclosed very much ground for such a course. If that man chose to go into United States territory and commit a crime, if he were properly apprehended there, I do not see any reason why we should attempt to set the power of our Government in force to release him except on ordinary humanitarian principles. But I am about to make a statement of fact, and remember that, coupled with it, I wish it to be clearly understood that I never did believe and do not now believe that Kelly committed the crime of assaulting the customs officer or that the customs officer was justified in going to the extreme length he did in firing upon Kelly under the provocation offered. I wish to read an affidavit made by Kelly while he was incarcerated in the county jail at Portland, Maine, prior to his trial, in order to give the House Kelly's side of the case and the reasons why, in my opinion, this House and this Government should take some action in order to see if the man cannot be released from his imprisonment. He has been in prison now for four years and he has certainly paid all the penalty that any man should be compelled to pay for the assault made upon the customs officer as I have described it, and I have not minimized the offence as far as Kelly was concerned; on the contrary, I have rather given every bit of evidence which could be given against him. This affidavit was prepared by a very responsible firm of solicitors whom we employed, Messrs. Drummond and Drummond. The affidavit is as follows:
State of Maine, County of Cumberland.
I, William J. Kelly, of the parish of Richmond, in the county of Carleton in the Province of New Brunswick, Canada, farmer, make oath and say:
That on Monday, the fifteenth day of Novem-

ber last past, a man calling himself Mr. Black, came to my residence in said parish of Richmond and came into the field where I was ploughing and asked me if my name was Kelly. I told him that it was and he wanted to know if I owned a Jersey cow, and I told him I did, and he wanted to know if I would sell it. I told him I would and he asked me what I wanted for it. I told him $25. He then asked me if my little girl owned turkeys at the house. I told him 'yes', and would she sell them? I told him I thought so.
He then asked me what I would take the cow and turkeys over to Hodgdon for,
Hodgdon is the name of a town corresponding to what we would call in New Brunswick a parish, or in Ontario a township.	It is immediately	across the
boundary line, although not a commercial centre or anything of that kind. Houlton would be the commercial centre:
-and I told him I would not go at all; that I would not haul them across the line; that I had made a promise at the time of the Burns scrape that I would smuggle no more. I asked him if he had ever heard of the Burns scrape and he said he never had. I asked him if he knew Burns and he said he did not. I told him something about the Burns scrape, and presently he said he would take dinner with me and we went together to my house. We looked at the cow on our way to the house, and at the house we talked with my daughter about her turkeys. From my house I went with him to my son-in-law's house where the turkeys were. He took his dinner there and asked me to take mine with him. I did so and he paid for both dinners. I left him there and went home and went to ploughing in my field again. He returned about two o'clock in the afternoon of that same day while I was still in the field ploughing and wanted me to drive him to Debec.
Debec would be the nearest railway station on the Canadian side of the line.
I drove him to Debec and left him and went home.
He paid me $1. About eight o'clock the next morning, Tuesday, November 16, he came back to me in the field again and asked me what I would take the cow and turkeys and a tub of butter and some chickens he had bought over to Hodgdon for. I again told him I would not cross the line on any consideration with them. He then asked me if I would haul them to the line and said he had a team engaged to meet him there. I told him that I would haul them to the line for $4. I was to make a box for the turkeys and chickens and help him pack them up for that sum and take them to the line. He said he was going down the road to get more chickens and look at some geese and would be back about one o'clock. He came back at about 1.30 or 2 o'clock and I was in the barn making a box for the turkeys and chickens. I then went with him to John Kirkpatricks and to Mr. Carrs and to Mr. Bearitos and got the butter and chickens and turkeys and we put them in the box. We loaded the stuff in my yard on the wagon and he went to my son-in-law's house for his supper. After supper he came back to my house and at this time he paid me $20 for the cow. I told him

I wanted $25 as the cow was my wife's, but he said he would pay the balance when I got it over to the line as I might get scared and not deliver it as X had agreed. This balance was to include the $4 for my picking up the stuff and hauling it over to the line. At this time I said to him: ' Now there will be no misunderstanding about this; that I would/ not drive my team over the line.' My wife was there and my family ' and heard me say so. This was about 7 o'clock in the evening. Presently we started with my team and two horses,-a white horse and dark bay horse,- in a sloven wagon, picking up some chickens on the road. We went by what [DOT] is called the Lower Hoad by Appleby's mill and reached Union Corner, which is in said parish of Richmond, and near the point where the highway road and international boundary line run parallel on the north at about 10 o'clock in the evening. As we were passing what appeared to be some bushes standing near Union Corner on the American side of the international boundary line he asked me what it was and I told him that I thought it was a wind-break, and shortly after that a man appeared on the road behind us. We then followed along the highway road, going north where the highway road is parallel with the boundary line but entirely on the Canadian side of the line, a distance, I should say, of about one-third of a mile, and I looked behind and saw the man hereinbefore referred to following, and finally I pulled my horses to the right-hand side of the road and stated that I would go no further. All of this time Mr. Black was on the wagon with me and he told me to get my horses back in the road. I pulled them further out of the road and got to a point just beyond where the ditch of the road^ ought to be, although it is my impression "that there was not any pronounced ditch at that point. This point would be a few rods north of the last post making the international boundary line before the road reaches that is called Crane's Corner, where it turns westerly across the line into the state of Maine. Immediately thereafter Mr. Black grabbed mo by throwing his arms around my neck. I at once grappled with him and we both rolled off the wagon. Black then called to the man whom I had seen following behind to come quick. I had recovered my feet when this man behind came up and grappled with him too and a scuffle ensued. I did everything in my power to regain my liberty but to no avail. The two men finally handcuffed me and together they loaded me into the wagon, and gagged me and the second man got astride of me. Black drove the team and carried me back into the highway road and got across the international boundary line into the town of Hodgdon. The next day I was brought to Portland and lodged in jail, where I am now confined. The man who came up from behind and who took me to Houlton and brought me to Portland I believe to be one Stevens, an officer of the United States Government, connected with the Revenue Department.
I may say, Mr. Speaker, that he is right in that, because Stevens was present at the trial and there was no doubt about Stevens being the man who followed behind him.
I am well acquainted with the road from Union Corner north to Crane's Corner, and when I was assaulted and arrested, as hereinbefore described, I must have been at least

ten rods south of Crane's! Corner and the whole, or at least a part, of my wagon was all the time east of the ditch on the east side of the road, and at no time was I over on the American side of the international boundary line. When we reached, as I thought, Crane's Corner, I heard two shots from a revolver and saw the shots go in the air, and I heard some one say ' What's this? ', and then another man whom I had not seen before on that night, got on the team and took the reins. Mr. Black then left and I saw no more of him. We drove on towards Houlton, with Stevens still holding me, for about twenty or thirty rods, I should think, when Stevens said that where was a team following, and leaving me in charge of the man who got on at Crane's Corner, Stevens went back on the road ; in about ten minutes Stevens came back and said the team had gone. We then went on toward Houlton, as I have before stated. Stevens called this man who got on at Crane's Corner ' Mr. Peters.'
(Sgd) William J. Kelly.

IE that is true, a very serious state of affairs is disclosed, and unfortunately I have no very great amount of evidence as to its truth or falsity. I have here the affidavit of a man named Read, an American citizen and a resident of the town of Houlton. This affidavit was drawn up on the 10th February, but the information was given very much earlier than that. It is short, and I shall read it because it is practically all the direct corroboration which we have in the form of an affidavit. It is as follows:
State of Maine county of Aroostook, to wit:
I, George E. Head of Houlton in the state of Maine one of the United States of American, painter and paperhanger, make oath and say:
1. That on the sixteenth day of November last, past, I started from the said town of Houlton to come to Union Corner in the parish of Richmond in the county of Carleton, in the province of New Brunswick, and was driven from said Houlton as far as Lincoln's Corner, so called, in the said state of Maine, and from said Lincoln's Corner I started to walk to the said Union Corner.
I may say that the distance between these two points would not be more than a mile.
I walked along from Lincoln's Corner the
greater part of a mile expecting that possibly I might meet on the road a friend whom I was going to see at Union Corner, Thadeus J. Furze, whom I knew would be returning from said Union Corner in a single team. T noticed ahead of me a turn in the road and after glancing along the road and seeing that there was no team near the corner or turn in the road,. I decided to cut across the field and strike the road beyond the turn. This was about 9 o'clock at night by Houlton time. I had got the greater part of the way across the field when I noticed a double team coming down the road leading from Union Comer. I stopped and watched the team. It was a double team, one horse a dark colour and the other a grey horse, and following behind the sloven wagon was a cow or a bull and also a man walking behind the wagon and there was a man driving. As I stood there I heard one of the men say * why don't you keep in the road,' and then I saw the team drive to the right into a field on the Canadian side of the road and go about two rods into the field. This would be about thirty rods from where the road turned to the left going to Houlton, and would be about three rods east from a granite post standing on the boundary line between New Brunswick and the state of Maine. About the time the team stopped I heard somebody shout * oh.' I looked up and saw a struggle going on between the two men that I had previously seen as I have mentioned. This struggle was on the ground near the team. I immediately noticed two men running from the corner that I have mentioned toward the team, and one man shouted as he came, * seize him by the legs.' These two men soon arrived at where the struggle was occurring and seemed to take part in the struggle. After a very few minutes the struggle ceased and a man was placed on top of a box which was on the forward part of the wagon. The other three men got on the wagon and the team was driven toward the American side down into the road and around the corner to the American side, then up towards Lincoln's Corner aforesaid, and went on up the hill, and passed out of my sight. I then started on my way again striking the road when I had passed through the corner of the field and noticed a single team going toward Union Corner.
That would be downhill going north to the corner where the road turns westerly
into the state of Maine.
I walked fast and overtook this team and found it was Thadeus J. Furze aforesaid and found that he had been driving from Union Corner but had turned about the time the double team had gone over the hill as aforesaid, and was going back toward Union Corner. Later in the same evening Mr. Furze and I went to Houlton, and I went to my boarding house and Mr. Furze went to his home.
(Sgd) George Edward Read.

In witness whereof, I, the said notary public, have hereunto set my hand and affixed my seal

That sums up all the evidence which we have in the form of affidavits as to [DOT] really what happened. We have never yet received any statement from the American officers, and there is no doubt whatever that they were officials, because this Mr. Black had been a sheriff and lived about thirty miles away from Union Corner. The other was Mr. Stevens, who is a United States deputy marshall, and has charge of investigating and prosecuting smuggling all along the boundary of the state of Maine. There is no doubt about the fact that Kelly was inveigled into the state of Maine. The only question of fact that is not absolutely settled is whether or not Kelly was taken there or whether he was taken in Canadian territory, true, within two or three rods of American territory, bound, gagged and hauled across the border into American territory as he describes.
We have a little more evidence, something that, while it is not in the form of an affidavit, is evidence nevertheless, because, you can understand, that a great hue and cry arose up and down the border next morning at this unfortunate occurrence. I was telephoned for from Houlton, and the officials in Woodstock, the sheriff and the deputy sheriff and everybody who was thought to have any authority, were telephoned for, and all went over. They were told by Kelly's friends that Kelly had been able to get into conversation by telephone with them, and I must say that the American authorities acted very fairly with him in that regard; they allowed him to call up his friends by phone after he had been safely locked up in the Houlton jail, and he was able to tell them what had happened. If Kelly is prevaricating he commenced prevaricating at that time, because at that time he told practically the same story that he told in this affidavit after being incarcerated at Portland some two months afterwards.
A great deal of excitement was created, and a great many people were there that day. There is no doubt in the world that the wagon tracks were there just exactly as Kelly had described them. It was in November and-the ground was -soft, so that when the wheels sank into the earth the marks were left and were visible. Any one could see that a fairly heavily loaded wagon had turned off on the right and had

gone beyond the ditch, because the tracks were there. There is no doubt that the people who visited the -spot saw the tracks, and I think the minister has in his department to-day-if not they had been sent to Washington-a number of photographs taken from all points of the compass bearing upon this road, showing the tracks, showing this corner and -showing the granite posts marking the international boundary line. The photographs -showed the existence of these tracks next morning just exactly as Kelly had described them in telephoning from the Houlton jail.
Mr. LANiCASTER: As I followed the affidavit, Kelly does not say Whether the American officers produced any warrant or not. Does the hon. gentleman know whether or not they claim to have' had a warrant when .they arrested him?

subtopic: THE CASE OF WILLIAM J. KELLY.
speechtext: I have never heard any mention of a warrant either by Kelly or the officials.

subtopic: THE CASE OF WILLIAM J. KELLY.
speechtext: He does not mention a warrant?

subtopic: THE CASE OF WILLIAM J. KELLY.
speechtext: No; there was no warrant.

subtopic: THE CASE OF WILLIAM J. KELLY.
speechtext: They did not pretend to have a warrant?

subtopic: THE CASE OF WILLIAM J. KELLY.
speechtext: No, I think they proceeded on the ground that he had committed a crime against their laws six years before, and onoe having got him within American territory, no matter how they got him there, they arrested him.

subtopic: THE CASE OF WILLIAM J. KELLY.
speechtext:
But according to
Kelly's statement, there is a question as to whether he was in American territory or not.

subtopic: THE CASE OF WILLIAM J. KELLY.
speechtext: That is the whole question. Kelly claims that he was assaulted, bound, gagged and dragged into American territory. I am trying to give to the House and to the minister all the evidence which we believe will substantiate Kelly's story. As I said a moment ago, the American officials have maintained an absolute silence on this question. We have never been able to get from them their side of the story. They have never made an affidavit as far as we know. They would not allow us to cross-examine these witnesses in court during Kelly's trial at Portland.

subtopic: THE CASE OF WILLIAM J. KELLY.
speechtext: As to these matters?

subtopic: THE CASE OF WILLIAM J. KELLY.
speechtext:
As to these matters. We were absolutely debarred from giving any

evidence pro or con as to what took place that night on the road, and all we have bearing upon that point is the affidavit of Kelly and the affidavit of this American, Read, and the fact of the existence of wheel tracks seen by many people next day and which were preserved by means of photographs. I think the minister has copies of these photographs here; at least, they were furnished to the department.
Mr. Speaker, you can readily understand that this created a great deal of excitement along the border, and when the man was convicted and sent to the United States prison at Atlanta we began to take steps to see if we could not have him liberated. It was a slow process, and finally, in the month of February or March, I got together all the affidavits I could. I got together probably half a dozen affidavits, which were presented to the American Government, but which are not worth reading here. For instance, there were affidavits from Kelly's wife and daughter that they were present and heard him absolutely refuse to go beyond the boundary line, and there were affidavits dealing with a number of collateral matters of that kind. I shall not take up the time of the House by reading them, because they would not be material to the case.

subtopic: THE CASE OF WILLIAM J. KELLY.
speechtext:
What did Black
appear to do with these goods that he purchased, or pretended to purchase, from Kelly?

subtopic: THE CASE OF WILLIAM J. KELLY.
speechtext: I do not know, I am sure. Kelly had received pay for them with the exception of $5.

subtopic: THE CASE OF WILLIAM J. KELLY.
speechtext: Is there anything to show whether Black was bona fide in making these purchases, or was it a trick to get Kelly into the United States?

subtopic: THE CASE OF WILLIAM J. KELLY.
speechtext:
It was a trick, but he bought the goods, paid for them, took them over into the state of Maine and disposed of them. I think an affidavit states what became of them. The cow was taken to a farmer just near the boundary line, and later on the cow was released under instructions of the chief customs officer of that portion of the state of Maine. The goods were taken into the state of Maine, and taken charge of by the officials who, I presume, sold them or used them. I am of the opinion, although I have no evidence of the fact, that the $5 which remained unpaid was sent to Mrs. Kelly later on.
Mr. LANCASTER [DOT] By Black?

subtopic: THE CASE OF WILLIAM J. KELLY.
speechtext:
By Black or some of the American officials. There is no doubt in the world that it was a trick of the American officials to get Kelly inffi thrir possession and they succeeded. I attempted to get the Government to ta&e this matter up some time in the early part of 1910 and I filed with the Government copies of the affidavits I have read here and perhaps hall a dozen more, giving to the department every particle of evidence which I had scraped together which was intended to substantiate the case put forward by Kelly.
I also furnished the department with copies of these affidavits and asked them to take the matter up with the British Ambassador in Washington in the effort to have Kelly liberated, but I do not know what happened. I know that international matters of this kind naturally move very slowly. I was told by the ex-Minister of Justice that they wanted more information but that was in a verbal conversation with Sir Allen Ayles-worth. I could not get any further information and I then made the proposition that the Canadian Government should endeavour to induce the American Government to appoint a commissioner to proceed to the spot or the locus in quo and make an investigation for himself. It is pretty hard to investigate an important international matter of this kind just on affidavits. I had an idea that if a commissioner could be appointed by the United States Government, that if our Government would also appoint one to act jointly with him and that, if together, they visited the neighbourhood and got their evidence at firsthand, they would be in a position to come to some reasonable conclusion as to whether Kelly was kidnapped, or whether he attempted to drive across the boundary line or whether he did drive across it. Even if Kelly deliberately drove the team across the line, he was not more than two or three rods on the other side, a fact which will not be denied by the United States customs officers.
Up to September, 1911, when the change of Ministers of Justice took place, I had not been able to accomplish my purpose. A good many things have happened in connection with this unfortunate case since I had any connection with it, and which I am sorry to say have not redounded to the credit of some of the men concerned. I do not think I would make my case complete, if I did not tell the House something about what has happened. In the first place, this matter was used as an election canvass, by my opponent in the general elections of 1911. I do not know

whether I lost any votes by it, perhaps I did, but whether I did or not one does not appreciate being charged with treachery to a client under such unfortunate circumstances as this man Kelly was placed in. A man would be venial indeed, who for any consideration in the world could be induced to betray a client who was in Kelly's position. However, that, is what 'I was charged with by my political opponents, and by no smaller a man than the Premier of New Brunswick. I would not have referred to this at all, were it not that it was also made a political football of at a later occasion, when an election for the New Brunswick Legislature occurred in 1912. I do not know what steps Mr. Fleming may have taken, in the meantime, but at all events he remained perfectly quiet about it from September 1911, until June 1912. When the local election came on then, he and his friends became very active again over the Kelly business. Kelly left at home a wife and nine or ten children. He had not more than an equity of $1,000 in his farm; his personal) property amounted to practically nothing; the family were kept together for a few months, and finally they had to break up their home. The farm was sold under a mortgage, and it was no fault of the mortgagee, because he would rather have lost the whole $1,200 than have distressed poor Mrs. Kelly in her trouble. However, she saw the impossibility of carrying on the farm. I think a relative worked the farm for her for a year, and then she asked the mortgagee to sell it and close the matter up. There is no fault to be found with the conduct of the mortgagee in the matter. The family were then scattered around amongst friends and relatives; three or four of them were old enough to earn their own living, and the poor woman went to McAdam Junction, about forty miles from her home, to keep some sort of a hoarding-house. That continued until the month of June, 1912, when Mrs. Kelly became seriously ill, and unfortunately departed this life, a' few days before the election. Her remains were brought home and she was buried in the Catholic cemetery at Debec, a day or two before the election.
What actually took place between Mr. Fleming and the Department of Justice I do not know, but I do know that it was the most beautifully staged political play, on such a sad occasion that I have ever heard of. The funeral took place about two o'clock in the afternoon, and a gentleman- who I am happy to say has been forced to 
leave the province of New Brunswick, I hope never to return-was sent post-haste in an automobile from Woodstock, just in time to arrive at Debec, eleven mi les away, when the funeral procession had been formed. He rushed up with hi3 automobile and handed a telegram to another gentleman named Fleming, who was a municipal councillor and a very important personage in that part of the country. He in turn handed the telegram to another gentleman named Kelly, an officer in the town of Woodstock, and this officer read the telegram over the open grave of this poor woman, her sorrowing children and friends standing around. All was planned and carried out with the greatest exactitude, simply for the purpose of making these people believe that the Premier of New Brunswick was trying to help the poor prisoner Kelly. I make the statement, and I am ashamed to have to make it, that it was all done purely for the purpose of gaining votes in the election which was to be held two days afterwards. Such a case of callousness; such a case of almost malice, is not to be found in the annals of Canadian history, and I hope nothing like it will ever happen again. I do not know what the telegram contained; I have tried assiduously for a year and a half to get the contents of that telegram, but I have not been successful. I have gone to the man who read it, and while I do not charge him with any duplicity, still he is not able to give me the telegram, and he says he does not know what has become of it. I have here a statement from a good old lady, the mother of a large family, who stood by the grave, and who heard the telegram read, .and I give you her version of it:
Debec Junction, February 13, 1914. Mr. F. B. Carvell,
Dear Sir,
As near as I can remember the circumstances, in re Kelly funeral, Owen Kelly told them not to bury Mrs. Kelly until William arrived, as he was now on the road, having been detained at McAdam Junction. Mr. Owen Kelly read the telegram to this effect.
Very sincerely yours,
Mary O'Donnell.
I hope the Minister of Justice will be able to throw some light on this. I have merely narrated the facts; I have shown you briefly what in my opinion is the most contemptible piece of political trickery ever heard of in the Dominion of Canada, and I pray to God that such a thing will never happen again. However, the body was buried, and whether the friends of the deceased believed it was a trick or not, I do

not know, but I think they did. I do not know that it made any difference in the result of the poll; I do not think it did; I rather believe the people refused to be caught in this way, and the burial took place that afternoon as had been planned. Of course, Kelly did not come home, and Kelly was not at McAdam Junction. But so far as I know, not a finger has been lifted by the Premier of New Brunswick from that day down to the present time to have this unfortunate man liberated. I do know that within the last three or four months, this same Mr. Kelly who read the telegram at the grave, and who is a relative of the prisoner, asked me if I would sign a petition praying the American Government to let Kelly out on ticket-of-leave, and I gladly signed the petition. I was surprised, when I was home only two weeks ago, to find that the petition had not been signed by anybody else, and the matter is dead so far as I know.
I want to appeal to the Minister of Justice to take some action, and I am doing this now when there is no election in sight; I am doing so, when I cannot be charged with trying to play the game of politics; I am doing it because I feel an injustice has been done to a British subject in the province of New Brunswick; I am doing it because now that there is no political excitement on, I cannot be charged with selfish motives. I believe something can be done for this poor man Kelly. I do not believe that the United States Government desire to play the part which Mr. Kelly in this affidavit says that they have played, and which, to a very great degre.e, has been corroborated by the evidence of one of their own citizens, Mr. George E. Read. I hope that if the Minister of Justice will take this matter up with the American authorities at Washington, he will be able to have an investigation. I think that might be done. I do not believe that the matter has ever been investigated. If it has, I have never been able to find that out as a fact. An investigation could be held, and if an honest investigation were held by a commissioner entirely removed from local prejudices and jealousies, I think that a statement of facts would be elicited that would convince the most callous that this man Kelly had been grievously wronged. His wrongs never can be righted. The man is now sixty-four or sixty-five years of age; his wife has died of a broken heart; his children are scattered to the four corners of the earth; his
property is gone, but the man would still have his liberty and the feeling that his country had done all in their power to vive him justice and to prove to him and his relatives and friends in that country eithtr that he is guilty of what the United States authorities claim he is guilty of, or that he is telling the truth and that he was really kidnapped as he says he was.
Outside of these two difficulties with the United States customs officers, no man in the province of New Brunswick ever bore a more exemplary character than Wm. J. Kelly, a man without an enemy, so far as I know, who never was in court, who never committed a crime or an offence, who was a sober, honest, industrious, hardworking Christian gentleman. You may say: Well, that is not the kind of a man who would commit such an act as you have described. A man must live along the boundary line to learn that people there do not consider it a crime to smuggle a load of potatoes, a few fowl or something of that kind across the border. It is an infraction of the law, and I am not trying to justify the offence: I am only giving the facts of the case. 1 think I am safe in saying that you would not find one in ten of the church deacons and even of the clergymen along the boundary line in the province of New Brunswick and the state of Maine who have not been guilty of an infraction of the customs law at some time or other in the course of their lives. That is a pretty broad statement.

subtopic: THE CASE OF WILLIAM J. KELLY.
speechtext:
Pretty broad.
Mr; CARVELL:	The people in the province of New Brunswick who will read these words of mine will say that I have placed the number too low instead of too high. Although Kelly probably knew that he was committing an offence against the customs laws of the United States, he did not consider it an offence to which would attach that degree of moral turpitude which would attach to any other infraction of the law.
In my opinion, the Minister of Justice owes it to a Canadian citizen, to a British subject, to start an investigation of some kind in order to satisfy the people all along that boundary line, no matter whether they be Kelly's friends or opponents-and I cannot see that Kelly has an opponent in the world-whether this man was kidnapped or whether he deliberately walked into this trap and placed himself under the jurisdiction of the United States courts. If he did the latter I have no fault to find. If he did not do the latter, but if he was kid-

napped, it is the duty of this Government-to do something in order to set the man right. The only suggestion that I can make is to ask the American authorities to appoint a joint commission to investigate this matter. If they will not do so, I would be satisfied if they would appoint one of their own commissioners to come up
5	p.m. here, go over that ground, take the evidence of the people whom we can produce, get the feeling in that country, get at the facts of the case. If they will do that, I believe that this man Kelly will be liberated and that as much of the injustice will be rectified as it is possible to do Tinder the very sad circumstances of this man and his family at the present time.

subtopic: THE CASE OF WILLIAM J. KELLY.
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman tell us when this occurrence took place? I was not able to follow him.

subtopic: THE CASE OF WILLIAM J. KELLY.
speechtext:
The 16th day of
November, 1909. The trial took place two months after that.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: THE CASE OF WILLIAM J. KELLY.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is quite right in stating that the Minister of Justice would realize that in a case such as he has described it would be incumbent upon the Government of this country to take some steps, at all events, to assure an investigation. I would like to point out that that was as true from the time that this thing happened up to 1911 as it has been since, and I am glad to add that in the time that elapsed before 1911, the hon. Minister of Justice of that date was quite awake to the desirability and the necessity of something being done in this regard, and that he did do something. After the change of government, the appeal to this Governor ent was again renewed. The renewal of that appeal came from the Government of New Brunswick through its Attorney General, from whom had come-my hon. friend the present Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) being at that time the Prime Minister of New Brunswick- the original appeal upon which the operations of the Minister of Justice of that day had been begun. Immediately after, not waiting for any local provincial elections at all, but towards the end of the year 1911, shortly after this Government had come into power, the Attorney General of New Brunswick again took the matter up with the Justice Department, and I think I shall be able to show to the House that if everything that could be done had not already been done by the previous Minister ' 
of Justice, no effort was spared by the present Minister of Justice and by the Secretary of State of this Government to bring about a result that would prove favourable to this unfortunate man; because, whether he was rightfully arrested in the United States or not, I am sure that we can all agree in sympathizing with the misfortune that has befallen him. He may possibly have deserved punishment,; but even where men deserve punishment, the punishment inflicted upon them may very well elicit sympathy, and I am quite satisfied that the records show that on the part of both the Minister of Justice at the time the occurrence took place and on the part of the Minister of Justice since it took place, there has been no lack of sympathy and no want of endeavour to bring about the liberation of this unfortunate man.
The last arrest of Kelly took place in 1909. On the 3rd of December, 1909, my hon. friend the present Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen), then Prime Minister pf the province of New Brunswick, communicated with the Department of Justice at Ottawa. I wish to give credit wherever it belongs, and I may say that about the same date my hon. friend (Mr. Carvell) also communicated with the Minister	of	Justice of	that day.
Their presentations made at that time were, in substance, the representations as regards the circumstances of the arrest which we have just heard from the hon. member. These were supported by affidavits- the affidvait of Kelly himself which, if I mistake not, was in the terms of the affidavit which the hon. gentleman has read, and also the affidavit of Mr. Read,-I have no doubt the same affidavit which the hon. gentleman has read. Basing himself on the action of the Prime Minister of New Brunswick, the then Minister of Justice, who, I may say, seemed to have considered that a strong prima facie case was made out in behalf of Kelly-and I do not think he was mistaken in that, having before him the evidence laid before him-reported to Council, and upon his report an Order in Council was adopted, and through the British Ambassador the matter was brought to the attention of the American Government. The American Government seem to have acted with a desire to verify the facts and to do justice in accordance with the findings as to the facts. They would appear to have named a special agent, who, so far as I can gather from his report, must have gone upon the ground and investigated this mat-

ter very thoroughly. He made a report, accompanying that report if I mistake not with the statements of the persons whom he examined. He furnished also a number of photographs of the place, as bearing, I take it, upon the statement made that the carriage containing the party at the time of the arrest had turned out on the Canadian side. Having gone into the details he reported to the Attorney General of the United States, if I mistake not, and his report was communicated to the British Ambassador and through him transmitted to this Government. As to that report, I find a memorandum on the file expressing the opinion of the then Minister of Justice to the effect that from the evidence adduced in this investigation-and from what is mentioned in it I would infer that in some way that had been communicated to the hon. member for Carleton, inasmuch as the minister makes mention of the desirability of such communication-

subtopic: THE CASE OF WILLIAM J. KELLY.
speechtext: If I am permitted, 1 desire to say that I received no such communication in writing from any one. X think Sir Allen Aylesworth spoke to me on the subject, and thought the chances of success were not very great. This is the-first I have heard of an American official being sent to investigate. If he did investigate, no Canadian official or authority, and no friend of Kelly's knew anything about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: THE CASE OF WILLIAM J. KELLY.
speechtext:
I do not wish to state it definitely, but I think a careful reading of the documents will show that this investigator did go upon the spot. But perhaps that is not material in view of what I have to point out as to what transpired afterwards. There is a memorandum of the 16th May, 1910, addressed to Mr. Power and signed by the deputy Minister of Justice, in which he says:
The minister passed these papers to me yesterday with the statement that he considered that the evidence produced with the United States reply preponderates, and that we probably cannot pursue the matter successfully. He desired, however, that a copy of the reply should he sent to Mr. Carvell, M.P., for any observations which he may desire to offer.
I have not gone all through the file, nor do I wish, the hon. gentleman having stated that he had no information, to imply that he had-

subtopic: THE CASE OF WILLIAM J. KELLY.
speechtext: What date?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: THE CASE OF WILLIAM J. KELLY.
speechtext: The 6th of May, 1910.

subtopic: THE CASE OF WILLIAM J. KELLY.
speechtext: I have no recollection of having received it. .

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: THE CASE OF WILLIAM J. KELLY.
speechtext:
I am not trying to make the point that the hon. gentleman had the information; all I am trying to show is that the Minister of Justice of that day seems to have been satisfied from the evidence given that the matter could not be pursued with hope of result. And the question dealt with in this investigation, as shown by the report, is the question where this man was laid hands on; it was not a question of his guilt or innocence that is referred to. I see nothing further with regard to the case until December, 1911. I am. not affirming positively that there is nothing, but am only giving the result of my examination of such papers as I have been able to find. In December, 1911, the Attorney General of New Brunswick again called the attention of the present Minister of Justice to the case. The case was again taken up through the British Ambassador, and there was a good deal of correspondence exchanged, with the result that the American Government caused another investigation to be made. I shall have a word to say in a moment with regard to the reports made in that investigation. As I have said, the matter was taken up in December, 1911, and was pending with the American authorities, I think, until October, 1912. The result was that the American Government informed the British Ambassador, and he communicated the information to this Government, that the matter had been gone over again by the American authorities, with a result similar to that which had been readied in the previous investigation. The last despatch that came bearing upon the subject I will give. It is a communication from the Acting Secretary of State to His Excellency the Ambassador, and dated the 11th of October, 1?1?-
The United States Attorney has informed ine Department of Justice that he has no hesitancy in saying that the allegation made by the prisoner's daughters that Kelly was forcibly abducted and taken across the line into the United States for trial is absolutely untrue;
That he has ample and reliable evidence to establish the fact beyond controversy that Kelly came across the line voluntarily for the purpose of committing the act of smuggling for which he was to receive compensation; that he was not arrested nor was any force used upon him until after he had come well within the borders of the state of Maine; that it was no fault of the prisoner's that he is not now serving a life sentence for murder.
He goes on to speak of the gravity of the* first offence, with which I do not think

we are concerned at the moment. Certainly there is no desire on my part to dwell upon that in any manner that might perhaps be injurious to this unfortunate man. I am quite sure that my hon. friend does not desire that I should. The result of that second action of the American authorities was as set forth in this letter from the ambassador, which was in answer to a telegram we had sent in October, at the instance of the Government of New Brunswick, pressing for action in the matter:
With reference to Your Royal Highness's telegram of October 16, 1912, and my reply thereto regarding the case of William Kelly, I have the honour to transmit herewith copy of a note received yesterday from the United States Government in reply to the representations in Kelly'S favour which 1 made in pursuance of Your Royal Highness' despatch No. 97 of August 14.
Owing to the absence of the Embassy in Washington, it has not been possible hitherto to take up the case personally with the pardon authorities of the Department of Justice. This will now be done with a view to effecting some arrangement, if such should appear feasible. Your Royal Highness will, however, observe that, from the nature of the case, the United States Government is provided with better evidence wherewith to support their contention than is now in the possession of the Embassy and that this is especially true with regard to the question whether Kelly was or was not on United States territory at the time of the arrest.
An official application for clemency on the double ground of irregularity in the arrest and of the destitution of the prisoner's family-
Because that has been put forward also.
-having now been officially refused, there are but two ways in which further effective action could be taken. Either the contention as to irregularity in the arrest must be supported by stronger evidence of a more exact kind, such as could form the basis of renewed official representations, or an unofficial and informal appeal can be made, based on general considerations of humanity, on the existence of strong local feeling in New Brunswick and possibly on the action of Your Royal Highness's Government in similar cases, involving citizens of the United States.
Until I am placed in a position to pursue the first course, I will follow the second alternative and will take such informal action as may be possible.
That was in October, 1912. To show that the matter was not dropped there and that the promise I have just read was carried out, in January 1913, we had a further communication from the Embassy, dated January 29, 1913, in which we were informed that His Majesty's Embassy had a copy of the report from the British Vice-Consul at Portland, Maine, embodying the result of an investigation made by him- under the instructions of -the Embassy into

the circumstances of Kelly's arrest. The ambassador writes:
The conclusions of this report do not appear favourable to any representations to the United States Government based on the circumstances of that arrest, but I should be glad to know whether, in the view of Your Royal Highness's Government, any further investigation would be desirable.
Your Royal Highness is doubtless aware that the question of Kelly's alleged abduction was the subject of correspondence between Lord Grey and myself in 1910.
The report of the consul shows that he himself went personally on the ground and made what would appear, from his report, to have been a very careful investigation.

subtopic: THE CASE OF WILLIAM J. KELLY.
speechtext:
Do I understand that
the report was made by the British ViceConsul?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: THE CASE OF WILLIAM J. KELLY.
speechtext: I understand that the report of Mr. Bagley, special agent of the United States, shows that he went on the ground. At all events after the American authorities had made the investigation which they thought proper, and which absolutely satisfied them, the British Ambassador, as the result of the communications we had had with them, caused an investigation to be made by the British Vice Consul at Portland.

subtopic: THE CASE OF WILLIAM J. KELLY.
speechtext: It is a most remarkable thing that no person in New Brunswick, none of the officers, none of Kelly's friends or relatives, no person concerned was ever notified. Of course, if the minister says it took place I presume it did, but it only shows that it was nothing short of a farce of an investigation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: THE CASE OF WILLIAM J. KELLY.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has told us he has no evidence on Kelly's side, but Kelly's affidavit, the affidavit of a man named Read and the affidavits of Kelly's relatives, which had no direct bearing on the question. That was the case that was put before the American authorities and it is the case as we have it upon which it is contended that Kelly was arrested on the Canadian side of the line. If the hon. gentleman can suggest anybody or any witness that might have been examined to throw further light upon this matter we would be glad to try to find a method of examining him.. But there is the case that was put forward by the hon. gentleman himself and there is the material in support of it; and I may say that the testimony sent with report and the report of the American investigation, to my mind quite justifies the view of the late Minister of Justice that the evidence of the United States preponderated and that this matter could not be

pushed further with any useful result. Notwithstanding that, at the repeated instance of the New Brunswick Government, we did try to push it farther and the final result was that the British consul at Portland made an investigation which satisfied himself that the arrest was made upon American territory. After stating that he went over the ground he says:	-
It has taken a great deal of time to connect with various officers and attorneys and obtain copies, etc., of the evidence and summarize the fullest particulars.
I have interviewed all the United States marshals and listened to the reading of the shorthand notes taken at the trial. In between times I quietly went over the ground travelled on the night of his arrest and I am, briefly speaking, of the firm opinion that there is every evidence to prove that this man was arrested when he was clearly on United States territory.
I enclose an extract of Kelly's own statement on the witness stand, also the particulars of his murderous assault. For sixteen years past I have frequently been passing and repassing the border-line. I am aware of the fact that the officers of both governments co-operate in the detection and arrest of confirmed smugglers. With this knowledge I carefully interrogated the officers who planned and carried out the * trap ' which Kelly fell into and I tried to get some evidence of overzeal, etc. Undoubtedly precise and full instructions were given to the officers to avoid the slightest infringement of international rights. The officers were particularly bright and clean set men. The instructions given to Deputy Stevens and officer Bragg were so definite that they were positively forbidden to arrest Kelly at or near the line. Mr. Smith, the deputy marshal, whom I have known for a number of years, and whose integrity is unquestionable, informed me that he even told the officers that if Kelly * shyed ' before getting well into the United States territory they were not to arrest him, and I am of the opinion that the officers were very careful to obey these instructions.
I am not going to take up the time of the House in reading all this report; but there is the situation. This matter has been investigated by the American authorities through the Attorney General's department, and there is the evidence and their report, concerning which I have given the opinion of my predecessor, which is also my own opinion. Not willing to drop it there, we have pressed the matter further. The American authorities have gone over it again, and have come to the same conclusion, and this has been confirmed by what looks to me a very painstaking investigation by the British Consul. 1 would be glad if it ceuld be shown to me that there is anything that can be done that would establish the facts to be as this unfortunate man Kelly contends they aTe, but both my predecessor and myself have
done the very best we could with the material we had at our disposal, and the American authorities have, I think, shown every disposition to look into the facts and not to take a one-sided position on it. We find that their investigation is confirmed by the investigation of the British Consul.
I must confess that for myself I am at a loss to see what further it is possible for this Government to do in the direction of claiming that Kelly is wrongfully _ imprisoned, and should, as a matter of right, be discharged because he was arrested on Canadian territory. Whether we can add any further weight to any further application for clemency that can be made on behalf of Kelly, is perhaps a question. I need only say that we will be very glad indeed _ to do anything we can do that may add weight to representations of that kind. We have done everything that is humanly possible to do. If Kelly be right in his statement that be was taken by force on the Canadian side, it is unfortunate, but it does not seem to me that there is proof of that, whereas upon the other side you have the evidence of a number of witnesses actually present, and who have been examined not only by the American authorities but by the British Consul, and unless we are prepared to take the position that these American officers are necessarily liars because they are officers, the evidence does, as Sir Allen Aylesworth says, preponderate absolutely in favour of the American contention. As pointed out by the Embassy, their position is just what would naturally happen. These American officers went out to inveigle Kelly to go across the line, and when they got him across to arrest him. They went out with the idea in their minds that they must observe just the exact circumstances in order to be in a position to say that they did not lay hands on him till he was in American territory. Unless you assume them to be absolutely lying, they are in a position to know and they are more in a position to know than anyone except Kelly himself. There is the testimony. I do not argue for its being well founded. I will be glad if the hon. gentleman can show me a ground on which I could urge that it is not. If such a ground could be shown I would urge it with all the force in my power. But I cannot at the present moment see, nny more than my predecessor Sir Allen Aylesworth could see, how I can, upon the evid-

enee available, establish anything to the contrary of the conclusion arrived at in these previous investigations. If any suggestion could be made of any means by which I, personally, or this Government could do anything to help this man to obtain clemency I would be very glad indeed, and I am satisfied the Government would be very glad, to give him that aid.
Now, to deal with the telegram. I do not understand that the hon. gentleman imputed anything derogatory to this department in that connection.

speechtext:
Might I then be excused for suggesting that if that be true there is an arena in which this question might be brought up-an arena where it would be more creditable to the courage of the hon. member to bring it up if he could find means of bringing it up there. The New Brunswick Government is not here, Mr. Fleming is not here, and the gentlemen who are charged are not here, and very naturally there is nobody here to meet the statements made. But may I point out the facts? A gentleman named Owen Kelly stated that Mr. Kelly was on his way there and suggested that the funeral be stopped. He read a telegram to that effect. But I am not in a position to say how it was connected with the New Brunswick Government; it is absolutely impossible for anybody here to meet what after all is a pure insinuation so far as the Government of New Brunswick is concerned. I think this file makes manifest that the hon. gentleman was wrong when he said that it was only when the provincial elections were coming on that the Attorney General of New Brunswick became interested in this case. The file shows that from the outset the Government of New Brunswick had set this matter in motion, and it shows that shortly after this Government came into power the Attorney General of New Brunswick, as early as December, 1911, took the matter up with this Government and set the machinery to work. That was a long time before the provincial election in-New Brunswick, and the insinuation that this telegram was the result of any sudden zeal developed by the Government of New Brunswick in view of a coming election is clearly unfounded, in face of the fact that they were interesting themselves in that matter at least since November, 1911-'if we are to deal only with the period this Government has been in power-and had 
been interested in it since December, 1909. So far as this Government is concerned, certainly no telegram was sent from anybody connected with this Government, susceptible of the same meaning as the telegram read at the funeral of this unfortunate woman. Just about that time the wife of this man Kelly was taken very ill. Her death was anticipated. The matter was brought to the knowledge of the Attorney General of Ne^ Brunswick, and what was the result? On the 12th June, 1912, the Premier telegraphed to the Secretary of State setting forth the facts which have been referred to by my hon. friend, that Mrs. Kelly was ill unto death, and pleading that an additional effort be made to get a ticket-of-leave for this man.

Exactly, and two days before Mrs. Kelly died. I suppose the hon. gentleman would suggest that her illness and death were all arranged as a part of the scheme. People die at election time and there are men who have courage enough to show sympathy with dying people even at election time, even though they have to face the possibility of large minded people taking their action as a basis for imputations such as the hon. gentleman is pleased to make against the Government of New Brunswick. Mr. Flemming sent this telegram :
William Kelly, of Richmond, N.B., was convicted about two years ago for assault on customs officer and for smuggling and sentenced to Atlanta, Ga., to prison for fourteen years ; there has been serious doubts whether he was arrested in the United States, it being strongly claimed he was on British soil when arrested. His wife is now seriously ill with an incurable disease and will probably not live more than a month. He has nine helpless children. Will you not make earnest appeal on his behalf; humanity calls for his being allowed to see his wife before she dies. Feeling very strong that he should be liberated on ticket of leave. Kindly appeal to President Taft if necessary.
The hon. gentleman suggested that Mr. Flemming, instead of sending that message, should have remembered tha,t there was an election on and that there were people capable of twisting fiis charitable action and imputing it to some of the motives which the hon. gentleman is prepared to impute to Mr. Flemming and his officers. But Mr. Flemming did not; he sent this mes-

sage and I think every one will say that he did the right thing even if it brings down the condemnation which has been visited upon him to-day. That was followed by the answer of the Secretary of State acknowledging it. The Secretary of State at once put himself in communication with the Governor General by whom a message was communicated to the embassy and through them to the American authorities, and as a result of the sending of that message there came a message from the embassy on the 15th June to the following effect:
Referring to your telegram 11th June, United States must be informed where Kelly will go if released on ticket of leave. Is his wife at Richmond? Telegraph reply with least possible delay to Percy, 26 East Erie street, Chicago.
Xnnes.
I suppose the hon. gentleman will take the responsibility of suggesting that Mr. Innes was in this deep laid plot. Mr. Innes, I may say, is the officer next in authority to the British Ambassador at Washington. That message was communicated, just as it stood, to the Attorney General of New Brunswick by the Secretary of State:
Referring to your telegram of 10th June instant re application for release of William Kelly, of Richmond, N.B., United States Government must be informed where Kelly will go if released on ticket of leave and also if his wife is at Richmond. Answer immediately.
There came back to that this answer from Mr. Flemming:
Telegram received. William Kelly's wife died yesterday. Nine children without any one to care for them. Kelly would no doubt desire to come home to Richmond, N.B., if released.
