The 18th June, 1912.
After that the Secretary of State continued in correspondence with the embassy and through them with the American authorities. During the course of that correspondence a number of letters were received from Mr. Flemming urging activity in connection with the matter. This was after the election was all over. He was just as energetic after the election as he had been before and just as much interested and it was with regret that we got the despatch of October, 1912, announcing the decision of the American Government and subsequently the report of the investigation by the British Consul at Portland.
There may be on this file some communications which may be confidential from the
point of view of other matters, but there is no objection to produce the papers bearing upon this question, so that my hon. friend may have an opportunity of perusing them.
I hope that after this statement and after being made aware of what these papers disclosed, he will be fair enough to recognize that the Premier of New Brunswick and my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries have shown no indifference to the claims of this man, and that he will likewise be fair enough to say that after this Government came into power, notwithstanding this memorandum that was not encouraging, we did take the matter up with energy and that we did the best that was in our poweT to bring about a result favourable to this man. It is neither the fault of my predecessor in office, nor my fault, nor the fault of this Government, that the evidence should preponderate against this unfortunate man. We did our best to make a case for this man with the evidence that was available. If the hon.. member can suggest any further evidence that will be of use I shall have much pleasure in doing my best to make the best use out of it, but I think that my hon. friend will admit that we have endeavoured to do everything that could be done with the material at our disposal. The appeal, in so far as it was an appeal to this Government to do something, was not unanswered.
In regard to the incident that happened at the time of the death of this unfortunate man's wife, who perhaps, very fortunately for the argument of the hon. gentlemen, happened to die a couple of days before the election, I hope, in view of the explanations contained in these two telegrams, that my hon. friend will be generous enough to acquit the man whom he was ungenerous enough to attack this afternoon and who has had no opportunity of defending himself.
Hon. J. D. HAZEN Minister of Marine and Fisheries): Mr. Speaker, I feel that as this matter appertains to a case that arose in the province of New Brunswick, and one with which I had something to do when I was Premier and Attorney General of that province, and with which I have had something to do since coming to Ottawa as a member of the present Administration, it is only proper and right that I should say a few words in Tespect to it. I listened to tire first three-quarters of the case as presented by the hon. member for the county of Carleton, (Mr. Carvell) with a great deal

of interest and I -was impressed with the clarity and fairness with which the hon. gentleman presented the question down to a certain point. I could not help feeling very great regret that at that point in his address the hon. gentleman indulged in a line of criticism which might justify any one in coming to the conclusion that in bringing this matter 'before Parliament and the country he was more anxious to score against a political opponent in his own county and province than to advance the interests of the man whose case has been brought to the attention of the House.
My attention was first called to this case of William Kelly in 1909, when I was Attorney General of New Brunswick. I received a letter from a Roman Catholic clergyman of Debee, Father Murphy, telling me of the circumstances of Kelly's arrest, and appealing to me for any assistance 1 could possibly render, as Attorney General of the province, to have Kelly relieved from the most unfortunate position in which he had been placed. I acknowledged that letter from Father Murphy, and curiously enough I find my original letter here on the file of the Department of Justice. How it came to be on this file I do not know, but it is the original letter, on the letterhead of the Prime Minister's Department of the province, and signed by myself. I wrote to Father Murphy on the 22nd of November, 1909:
St. John, N.B., November 22, 1909. Rev. M. T. Murphy,
Debec, Carleton county, N.B.
Dear Father Murphy,-I am in receipt of yours of the 20th instant, with regard to ' your unfortunate parishioner ' and my countryman, Mr. William Kelly, who is now lying1 in Portland jail. It would certainly appear from your letter as if means were used to induce Kelly to cross the line which were, td say the least, of very doubtful character, still we all know that detectives do resort to such means, and if Kelly was actually induced to go across the line and was arrested there, the authorities in Maine would be quite within their right in doing so; if, however, he was forcibly taken possession of on the New Brunswick side of the line, hauled over into Maine and1 then arrested, the question assumes an entirely different complexion, and steps might be taken through the Department of Justice at Ottawa, and through my own department as Attorney General of New Brunswick, to have the wrong that was thereby created set right. In order to accomplish this, however, the first thing that will be necessary it seems to me is to obtain evidence to the effect that Kelly was forcibly dragged across the line into the state of Maine. With such evidence we would know-where he stood and his only course without it would be to get a lawyer and have himself defended as well as possible when the case comes to trial.
It would seem about incredible that Kelly should have gone willingly across the line in
[Mr. Hazen. 2
view of the statement which he made to his wife to the effect that he 'would not haul the produce across the line for $1,000, no, not foil all Houlton."
I think the best course for Kelly's friends to take is to consult a lawyer in Woodstock and obtain from him (Kelly) a statement} as to exactly what occurred so that we may know his version at least of what took place and whether or not he was arrested on the New Brunswick side of the line. It would also be well, I think, to have all the facts communicated to Mr. Carvell, M.P., at Ottawa, so that he may bring the case to the attention of the Department of Justice.
I can assure you of my profound sympathy with you in regard to this matter and my desire if I possibly can be of service to Kelly and his friends in view to of the manner in which he was enticed away from home after having for years abandoned any business as a smuggler.
Tours very truly,
(Sgd) J. D. Hazen.
On the third of December, 1909, a short time after Kelly's arrest, I communicated with the Department of Justice, and curiously enough my letter to the department is not on the file, as it should be, but there is a letter from the Department of Justice to me, acknowledging the receipt of that letter, and it reads:
December 9, 1909.
Dear sir,-I am directed by the Minister of Justice to acknowledge receipt of your letter of 3rd instant, relative to the case of William Kelly, alleged to have been kidnapped to the United States from the province of New Brunswick.
The matter is at present receiving the attention of the department, and Father Murphy has been requested to obtain the requisite evidence in order that the matter may be brought to the attention of the United States Government.
I have the honour to be, sir,	[DOT]
Tour obedient servant,
(Signed) A. Power,
for D.M.J.
Hon. J. D. Hazen,
Attorney General,
St. John, N.B.
Then follows on the file a letter from the department to Mr. Carvell, dated December 17, though Mr. Carvell's letter does not appear to be on file. There is also a letter from Mr. Carvell, dated 20th December, asking that the documents in reference to the Kelly matter should be held until he is again heard from, and he states he hopes to get further information. On January 3 there is a furtjiei. letter from Mr. Carvell, enclosing another affidavit in the Kelly matter, which he asks should be put with the other documents, and he is still in hope of obtaining further affidavits. On January 18 a report was made to Council, upon which an Order in Council is ba^ed, that report being signed by Sir

Allen Aylesworth, then Minister of Justice. Tt- reads:
January 18, 1910.
To His Excellency the Governor General in Council:
The undersigned has the honour to submit a corfimunication from the Attorney General of New Brunswick, dated the 3rd ult., in connection with the forcible abduction from Canadian territory by officers of the United States Government, or of the Government of the state of Maine, of one William Kelly, of Richmond, New Brunswick, also three affidavits and two declarations under the statute with reference to the affair, and eight photographs illustrating the locus. Kelly is now said to be In custody in the state of Maine awaiting trial on a charge of assaulting a United States customs officer six years ago, a charge for which he was tried in New Brunswick at the time, and of which he was found not guilty.
From the affidavits and declarations submitted, there appears to be every reason to believe that the United States, or date officers came into Canada and, without any authority of law, forcibly seized a Canadian citizen and took him into the United States against his will.
The undersigned has the ..onour to recommend that the communication of the Attorney General of New Brunswick, as well as the affidavits, declarations and photographs referred to, be transmitted to His Majesty's Ambassador at Washington, to the end that such representations may be made to the Government of the United States as shall secure that Kelly be at once set at liberty, so that he may return to his home, reserving, in the meantime, the discussion of the questions of reparation and compensation.
(Signed) A. B. Aylesworth,
Minister of Justice.
An Order in Council, baaed upon the report to Council made by Sir Allen Aylesworth, was passed and that Order in Council is attached here, being couched in practically the same terms as the report to Council. This Order in Council was forwarded to the British Embassy at Washington.
In passing, I would like to call attention to the fact that in December, 1909, when there was no prospect of any election in New Brunswick for years to come, I, as Attorney General of New Brunswick, took the action upon which Sir Allen Aylesworth based his report to Council, asking the United States authorities to have this matter looked into, with a view of seeing that justice and fair play was dealt out to the unfortunate man who had been sent to the penitentiary for this long term of imprisonment. My hon. friend (Mr. Carvell) has discussed this matter as though those who were endeavouring to bring about the release of Kelly, or those who were making representations to the Government in the matter, were actuated simply by a desire of making political capital and gain. I desire to say to my bon. friend, that when I got that letter from Father Murphy it appealed to my sympathies at once, for I felt that even if Kelly six years before had been guilty of smuggling into the United States, while it is a crime against the law of the country, yet, to a certain extent, it is, as my hon. friend stated, an offence which a great many people have indulged in on both sides of the line. I remember very [DOT] well the circumstances of the Kelly trial in the first instance, and I did not think there was justification on the part of the American officer in 1903 for drawing his revolver and firing twice at Kelly.
I felt that the action had not come to that point where it was necessary, in order to effect the arrest, that the officer should do so, and I felt under those circumstances that, a man being fired at twice and practically being struck twice, it was little wonder that his blood got up and that there were most extenuating circumstances for his assaulting the officer and giving him a very severe beating. I had those facts in my mind, but I had a further very strong appeal made to me in very strong, pathetic language by Father Murphy with regard to the condition of this man's unfortunate wife and family. Knowing these circumstances, and even if those circumstances had not existed, if there was a doubt as to whether this man had been arrested on the Canadian side of the line instead of on the American side, I would have felt it to be my duty to have that doubt dispelled and to bring it to the attention of Sir Allen Aylesworth, then Minister of Justice. I have pointed out to the House that it was on my communication to Sir Allen Aylesworth that he made the report to Council that I have read, on which the Order in Council was passed that set in motion the machinery of the British Consul at Washington.
Following along the file, and I do not want to take up much time with it because it has been referred to by the Minister of Justice, I find that Mr. Bryce acknowledged the receipt of the Order in Council and that he wrote a letter to the United States Secretary of State, Mr. Knox, as follows:
British Embassy,
Washington, February 7, 1910.
Sir,
I have received from the Governor General of Canada copy of an approved Minute of His Majesty's Privy Council for Canada together with certain documents regarding the forcible abduction from Canadian territory by officers

of the United States Government, or of the Government of the state of Maine, of one William Kelly of Richmond, N.B.
As will be seen from the affidavits and declarations enclosed herein, there appear good reasons to believe that on November 16 last Kelly was forcibly removed by these officers from the Canadian side of the international boundary in the province of New Brunswick and taken into the state of Maine, where he is now awaiting trial on the charge of assaulting a United States customs officer six years ago-a charge for which he was tried in New Brunswick at the time of the alleged assault and of which he was found not guilty.
I have the honour to request that you will move the proper authorities to make an immediate investigation into the circumstances attending the alleged abduction of Kelly, and that, should it be found that the statements contained in the enclosed declarations are in accordance with the facts of the case, Kelly may be at once released, reserving the question which may hereafter have to be considered whether or not he is entitled to reparation and compensation.
I have the honour to further enclose a list of the documents which accompany this note.
(Sgd) James Bryce.
It seems to me that the Government of my right hon. friend who leads the Opposition took the only course that .was open for them. They made these representations to the British Ambassador, and he communicated with the Secretary of State of the United States, with the result that the report was made to the proper officials of the United States and they found from the information before them that there was no cause for them to doubt that Kelly had been arrested on the United States side of the line, and they, therefore, refused to interfere. I do not see what other course the Minister of Justice of that day could have taken. Later on I will show that I do not see what further course the Minister of Justice of the present day could have taken after the matter was called to his attention by myself and others almost continuously from 1911 down to a few years ago.
At sir o'clock, the House took recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: THE CASE OF WILLIAM J. KELLY.
speechtext:
At six o'clock I had pointed out that the Government which preceded the present Government, had passed an Order in Council with regard to this matter a copy of which was forwarded, through the proper channels, to the British Ambassador at Washington. It would appear from the reply that the British Ambassador promptly took the matter up with the Secretary of State for the United States on the 7th of February. On the same day, he informed the Government in Ottawa that he
[Mr. Hazen.J
had the honour to transmit a copy of the note which he had addressed to the United States Government calling the attention of the Secretary of State to the forceful abduction of William Kelly on Canadian territory and requesting that the matter might "be inquired into forthwith by competent authority. The Minister of Jad:

3 has told us what occurred, of the correspondence which was received and the inquiry made into the matter in the United States and the conclusion come to by the United States authorities. He has also told us of the memorandum of the Minister of Justice of the preceding Government with regard to the subject. My hon. friend from Carleton evidently heard of that for the first time today, as I judge from the remarks he made. It is almost incredible to me that my hon. friend, if he had the interest in this case that he would have it believed he had, should not have known what was done with regard to it by the Government he supported. He was in this Parliament during the session of 1910 and the session of 1911, yet he knew nothing of what had taken place. One would imagine if he had any interest in the case that he would not have allowed a single session to pass without going to the Department of Justice, and discussing the matter with the minister, the deputy minister and the officials there and learning what had taken place. Yet, on his own admission, he did not know what had taken place, and so the conclusion is almost irresistible that he was not really interested in the case of William Kelly. He moved in the matter when approached, as I moved, as Attorney-General of New Brunswick when I was approached on the subject in November, 1910. But apparently he then allowed the matter to stand and did nothing further about it; and revives it now, when, having heard a rumour of some telegram about Mrs. Kelly's death and funeral he thinks he can make party capital against his fellow townsman who is now Prime Minister of New Brunswick.
We have the facts of what occurred down to the time when the Government supported by the hon. gentleman went out of power. The new Administration wais sworn into office on the 11th of October, 1911. I have a private file in my office with a number of letters bearing on the case and to isome of these letters I wish to ask the consideration of the House. In 1911, while I was at my home in St. John on the occasion of the Christmas festival, I was called on by Mr. Frank Smith, of Florenceville, in the

county of Carleton, a gentleman who has been a member of the Legislative Assembly of New Brunswick and came near being a member of the House of Commons, being defeated by only nine votes, if I remember well. He told me of the existence of intense feeling in the county of Carle-ton over this case of William Kelly. He said that the sympathy of the people irrespective of politics was with Kelly and that there was the greatest desire that he should be released from prison. Mr. Smith asked if something could not be done through Government intervention to get Kelly released that he might return to his wife and family and his home in Richmond, in Carleton county. I promised I would take the matter up with the Department of Justice. When I returned here, I found a letter from Mr. Kirkpatrick, who had been Trade Commissioner of the Dominion in the West Indies. I will just read a few sentences from Mr. Kirkpatrick's letter:
I have learned from Mr. B. Prank Smith that he has taken up through you the question of the case of William Kelly, a Canadian citizen, who is undergoing one of the most barbarous punishmehts in the United States federal prison that I have ever heard of. 1
I have known William Kelly quite intimately for a life-time and his only crime was that of being an inveterate smuggler. He was a struggling farmer having a wife and ten children to support. He was a sober and peaceful citizen and a man who was well liked by every one.
When the United States authorities sought to have him extradited a number of years ago on the charge of smuggling and assault, the late Justice Gregory who heard the case decided that there were no grounds on which he should be given up and was set free. Seven years later he was kidnapped and sentenced to fourteen years imprisonment while his wife was left in poverty with ten children to support.
I took the mutter up with the Minister of Justice and urged him to see if something could not be done in order that the sentence might be commuted or lessened, so that this man might return to jhis home. It has always seemed to me that fourteen years' imprisonment, the punishment meted out to him, was a punishment too great for the crime. And in view of what my hon. friend from Carleton said this afternoon, while he was most moderate in stating it, it would almost look as if there had been a breach of faith, in view of the understanding arrived at at Portland in giving the man four years' imprisonment for the old offence in addition to the ten years for the assault on the United States customs officer-an assault, I do not hesitate to say again, which was largely provoked by that officer himself, who, I think had no justification whatever in shooting at Kelly under the circumstances, and in view of that shooting Kelly did what any man, I think, would have done, assaulted . the officer believing he was doing it m defence of his own life. I had a strong letter from Mr. Frank Smith also in which he said:
'He Wm Kelly of Debec' I have received your favour June S enclosing copy of letter to you from E. S. Kirkpatrick of Debec. This is the case I talked with you about at your own home in St. John during the holiday. I asked Mr. Kirkpatrick to write you with regard to same, as he lives very near Kelly's home, and I felt that he knew quite a lot about the details of the case.
When I talked with you in St. John, we agreed that you would examine the flies of the Minister of Justice, when you went back to Ottawa, to learn exactly what progress had been made with this case under the Laurier Government.
If you will kindly do this, and take the case up with the Minister of Justice, I shall then be glad to work along the lines that you may suggest, and furnish you with the fullest detailed evidence.
It really is a most important matter that every effort should be made to liberate this man who was without a doubt kidnapped.
And I think that is the universal opinion in Carleton county; everybody you speak to there believes that the man was kidnapped and dragged over the line, though the American authorities refuse to believe anything of the sort and say they have complete evidence that the arrest took place on the American side. I understood my hon. friend from Carleton, who took part in the defence of Kelly in Portland, to say that the judge there ruled that he could not go into the evidence whether Kelly was on the Canadian or American side at the time of his arrest, contending that if he was in the United States, regardless of how he got there, he was within their jurisdiction, and that even if it were shown that he had been dragged over the line, that would be no defence against the charge brought against him and would not go in mitigation of the charge. I hope I have correctly repeated what my hon. friend said.

subtopic: THE CASE OF WILLIAM J. KELLY.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is quite correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: THE CASE OF WILLIAM J. KELLY.
speechtext:
That -being the case, if that view were taken by the higher authorities at Washington, then, even though the former Minister of Justice, Sir Allen Ayles-worth, and the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) had evidence in support of the contention made as to kidnapping those authorities, I assume, would not

regard that as suffiicent reason why Kelly should be given up or why he should be pardoned.
I understood my hon. friend to say that undoubtedly there was American authority that was produced on the trial to show that the contention made by those acting for the state, for the prosecution at the trial, and by the judge, was correct. Therefore, even if it had been demonstrated to the satisfaction of the authorities at Washington that Kelly was not arrested in the first instance on the American side of the line, but had been dragged over the line by forcible means, if the law as laid down by the learned judge who tried the case at Portland was correct law from the standpoint of the United States, the reason would not exist why they should give Kelly up and send him back to Canada.

subtopic: THE CASE OF WILLIAM J. KELLY.
speechtext: I do not wish my hon. friend or any member of the House to draw any inference as to what I stated except the actual facts of the case, because this may be brought to the notice of the United States officials and of Judge Hale, the presiding judge at Portland. I do not know that any authorities were quoted by either the prosecuting counsel or by the judge to substantiate that position. They simply took that position and maintained it, and absolutely refused to allow any evidence bearing on the question of how Kelly got into American jurisdiction. They simply said: He is here in our jurisdiction, an indictment has been found against him, and we are going to try him on that indictment.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: THE CASE OF WILLIAM J. KELLY.
speechtext:
I understood my hon. friend to say that there were American authorities. Of course, it may be said that in some encyclopedia of law in the United States you can get some authority from some state that will support almost any contention. It would seem to me, as an international matter, that no country would approve of its officials crossing the boundary into another country, absolutely kidnapping a man, taking him by foree across the boundary line, then arresting him and trying him on a charge six years old. I should think that if it could be proved to the satisfaction of the Secretary of State at Washington that this man had been kidnapped and by force dragged across the line and arrested and tried, the authorities of the United States, looking at it from the broad standpoint of international law and justice, would say that the man ought 
to be given up and returned to the country from which he came. That may or may not be the case, but that is the way it presents itself to me. But, at the same time, up to the present neither the Minister of Justice of the Laurier Government nor the present Minister of Justice nor any information that has been given to the State Departmefit at Washington, has convinced them that that was the case. On the contrary they have the opinion read this afternoon in the report from the British Consul at Portland, a man who investigated the matter, who \yent into the country and along the boundary line where the offence was committed, who makes a report certainly against the contention made by those on the Canadian side. Still I do not think there is a man in the county of Carleton who does not believe that the man was kidnapped and dragged across the line and was arrested when he got across the line. There is no doubt on this point, that the man was enticed to go near the boundary line by the action of detectives sent by the United States Government for that purpose. Of course, it may be said that that is a method that detectives generally adopt, and that they have a perfect right to do it, but it does seem a most harsh and cruel 'proceeding, six years after an offence for which a man was found not guilty in a court of justice in a British country, that he should, by means of that sort adopted by detectives, be taken across the boundary line and then arrested and taken off and sentenced to fourteen years' imprisonment for an offence of which he was practically acquitted when a court in New Brunswick refused to allow him to be extradited for the offence. Six years had passed since then, during which time he had been an exemplary member of society and a good citizen in the community in which he lived.
Referring to further correspondence which I had on this matter, I acknowledged Mr. Kirkpatrick's letter and took up the matter with the Minister of Justice. But I did more than that, I wrote a personal letter on the subject to the British Ambassador at Washington, the Right Hon. James Bryce. I ventured to do this because I have known Mr. Bryce quite a while. I had the honour of entertaining him at my house in St. John when he was in New Brunswick. He visited Ottawa afterwards, where I again met him and I had the honour of being his guest in Washington. He had told me here and in Wash-

ington if there was any matter of a personal character, apart from any official matter in my department, about which I wished to communicate with him, to write him a letter directly, a personal letter, and he would be only too pleased to take the matter up and to deal with it in the way that he thought best. Therefore, interested as I was and believing that an act of very great hardship had been done to the unfortunate man Kelly, on the 22nd of June, 1912, I wrote this letter to Mr. Bryce:
My dear Mr. Bryce:
Sometime ago a man named Kelly, a British subject, residing in New Brunswick, in the county of Carleton, was arrested by United States officials and taken to Portland and tried lor assaulting a customs officer, many years before, and sent to prison in the United States.
I understand the facts of the case have all been laid before you. There is very great local indignation felt in regard to the matter, and great sympathy for Kelly and his family. His wife died a few days ago and this makes the case exceedingly hard for his family. The universal belief in New Brunswick is that Kelly was on the Canadian side of the line and was forcibly dragged across into the United States at the time of his arrest. I am not going to weary you with a recital of the facts for, as I said before, I understand they have been submitted to you. I merely wish to say that if you can in any way bring influence to bear on the United States authorities to secure Kelly's release, then you will be doing an act which I believe is one of justice and mercy as well.
I am, yours very sincerely,
(Sgu) J. D. Hazen.
Let me say that about a week before this I had been approached in regard to the matter by a gentleman named John E. McCloskey, of St. John, an officer of the Inland Eevenue Department who died about a year ago, who was then secretary of the Ancient Order of Hibernians in New Brunswick. He told me the members of that order were very much interested in the case and he would be very much indebted to me if I could do anything to assist to bring the matter prominently before the authorities in Washington. On the 12th of June I received a letter from Mr. McCloskey in which he says:
I received the enclosed this morning. This makes the case extremely sad. Kindly return the letter.
It was a letter announcing the death of Mrs. Kelly. That was on June 12, eight days before the general election in New Brunswick; and I am quite sure that Mr. McCloskey had no thought in writing that letter of assisting any party in New Brunswick in the election. I wrote acknowledging the receipt of this, and it was a 109
few days later that I wrote the letter to Mr. Bryce to which I referred, personally asking him to interest himself in the matter as an act of justice and mercy. Mr. Bryce wrote back on the 28th of June, six days after the election, saying this:
My dear Mr. Hazen:
Many thanks for your letter June 22 regarding the man named Kelly. At the request of His Royal Highness the Embassy applied a fortnight ago for his release on ticket of leave.
That was the time Mr. Flemming sent a telegram here and it was forwarded to Washington.
And the matter is still under consideration by the Department of Justice at Washington. Some difficulty has been experienced owing to the fact that such ticket of leave would npt,
X understand, hold In Canada and the United States authorities would therefore have to trust to his honour to return. Mainly for this reason it was impossible to secure his release before his wife's death.
Then he suggests that he should be put in possession of all the facts in regard to the ease, as this would enable him to set on foot an application for his pardon. I think Mr. Bryce was mistaken in thinking the embassy was not in possession of all the facts, because the facts had been communicated to them, in the first place by Sir Allen Aylesworth as Minister of Justice, through the Department of the Secretary of State, and, in the second place, by the present Minister of Justice. There was some further correspondence. I wrote Mr. Bryce again, reminding him of the matter, and I wrote to Mr. McCloskey, and on the 25th of October, 1912, I received this from the Department of Justice:
I am desired by the minister to send you herewith, for your information, copy of a despatch of 16th instant from the British Ambassador, recently referred to this department.
Tours sincerely,
E. L. Newcombe.
That was a result of the representations made in Mr. Flemming's telegram and of the representations made by myself and by the Minister of Justice. It contains a copy of a letter to Mr. Bryce signed by Huntingdon Wilson, acting Secretary of 'State, which I will read:
Department of State,
Washington, October 11, 1912.
Excellency,-Referring to previous correspondence relative to the petition in behalf of William J. Kelly, a federal prisoner at! Atlanta, Georgia, convicted of resisting a United States officer and smuggling, I have the honour to inform you that a letter on the subject has been received from the acting Attorney General in which he states that Kelly brutally assaulted Mr. Frank Burns, a United

States customs officer, who was endeavouring to apprehend him while he was engaged in smuggling a load of merchandise into thid country; that he left Mr. Burns for dead and afterwards stated that he thought the man was dead and was sorry he had not finished the job.
The United States Attorney has informed the Department of Justice that he has no hesitancy in saying that the allegation made by the prisoner's daughters that Kelly was forcibly abducted and taken across the line! into the United States for trial is absolutely untrue; that he has ample and reliable evidence* to establish the fact beyond controversy that) Kelly came across the line voluntarily for the purpose of committing the act of smuggling' for which he was to receive compensation that he was not arrested nor was any force used upon him until after he had come well within the borders of the state of Maine; that it was no fault of the prisoner's that he is not now serving a life sentence for murder ; that the man's conviction has done more by force of example to quiet outlaws and pre-1 serve respect for this Government and itd officers along the border than anything that! has been done in the last 50 years, and that) to pardon the man now after only two years' imprisonment would undo all that has beenl accomplished.	.
While this Government greatly regrets the privations suffered by Kelly's family as a con-! sequence of his imprisonment it does not appear from all the facts and circumstances! in the case that the ends of justice would be subserved by the pardon of the prisoner.
I have the honour to be,
With the highest consideration,
Tour Excellency's most obedient, humble servant,
(Sgd) Huntingdon Wilson,
Acting Secretary of State.
There was a covering letter to that from the British Embassy, signed by A. Clark Kerr (for the Ambassador) which reads as follows:
British Embassy,
Washington, October 16, 1912.
Sir,-With reference to Tour Royal High-I ness' telegram of to-day and my reply thereto! regarding the case of William Kelly, 1 have1 the honour to transmit herewith copy of a! note received yesterday from the United States Government in reply to the repre-) sentations in Kelly's favour which I made inj pursuance of Your Royal Highness' despatch! No. 97 of August 14.
Owing to the absence of the Embassy in Washington, it has not been possible hitherto! to take up the case personally with the pardon' authorities of the Department of Justice. Thiif will now be done with a view to effecting! some arrangement, if such should appear1 feasible. Your Royal Highness will, however,' observe that, from the nature of the case, the' United States Government is provided with better evidence wherewith to support their* contention than is now in the possession of thd Embassy and this is especially true with re-' gard to the question whether Kelly was or! was not on United States territory at the! time of the arrest.
An official application for clemency on the double ground of irregularity in the arrest and of the destitution of the prisoner's family, having now been officially refused, there are'

but two ways in which further effective action' could be taken. Either the contention as tc< irregularity in the arrest must be supported' by stronger evidence of a more exact kind, such as could form the basis of renewed official representations, or an unofficial, and informal appeal can be made, based on general considerations of humanity on the existences of strong local feeling in New Brunswick and! possibly on the action of Your Royal Highness'' Government in similar cases, involving citizens of the United States.
Until I am placed in a position to pursue the first course, I will follow the second alternative and will take such informal action as may be possible.
I sent a copy of this to Mr. McCloskey who had been corresponding with me and to Mr. Smith of East Florenceville. Mr. Smith asked me to advise him what could be done and I wrote to him and Mr. McCloskey as follows:
31st October, 1912.
Dear Frank,-I am in receipt of yours of the 29th instant. I hardly know what to advise you with regard to the Kelly matter. Everything has been done, apparently, that can be done, up to the present time, but the authorities in the United States evidently feel very bitterly over the matter, and are not disposed to be lenient in their treatment of the unfortunate man. However, I presume they are humane as well as other people and in view of the death of Kelly's wife, might be subject to some influence of a personal character that might be brought to bear upon them.
How would it do to get up petitions in the county of Carleton and elsewhere throughout New Brunswick, setting forth, ,clearly and, well, the unfortunate circumstances in which Kelly's family are left, and have them presented through the British Ambassador at Washington? If it would be productive of any good, I would be willing myself to go to Washington with these petitions, and see the British Ambassador and the authorities of the United States, in regard to the matter. I can only do this in my personal capacity. I do nof think it would be proper to do so as a member of the Government, but I will gladly do so, and the fact that I am a member of the! Government would not in any way lessen the effect which my presentation of these petitions in my personal capacity might have. If you determine to get up petitions, and I only throw the suggestion out for your consideration-it should be done very thoroughly, and thousands of names should be obtained. From what I learned of the case I think the feeling against Kelly is very strong on the part of the United States authorities, and knowing as they must have known that he was watched for in consequence of his assault upon the American customs officer, years before, he should have kept away from the border, but I suppose he was .quite careless in consequence of the lapse of time, and thought that the' trouble was all over. Apparently, however, the man whom he assaulted, never let off his track and watched him for years for the purpose of bringing him to justice and having him punished. There is no use, however, harping on this; the thing is to get the man out of prison if it can be done, for the sake of his family, and I can conceive of no other step that can be taken. I understand that the members of the

Ancient Order of Hibernians are moving in the matter and that they can bring influence to bear through their society in the United States. ,T. R. McCloskey of St. John is secretary I believe of the Order. He spoke to me about the matter some time ago, and perhaps you might correspond with him and get his views as to what action had better be taken.
I had an acknowledgement from Mr. Smith saying he was corresponding with McCloskey. Unfortunately McCloskey died not long afterwards. I received, however, on January 16, last year, a letter from McCloskey enclosing a copy of a letter from Joseph D. Sullivan in which he refers to a meeting of the Ancient Hibernian officers in Washington and to having discussed the matter of Kelly's release with several of them at great length. He says:
The situation has not been materially changed. I called at the British Embassy in Washington1 and they advised me that they have no papers bearing upon this subject whatsoever except a letter received from Mr. J. D. Hazen of Ottawa.
That is absolutely incorrect and Mr. Sullivan must have been misinformed. All of this information was there. The letter concludes:
On my call at the British Embassy I was advised by one of the under-secretaries that! they would ascertain from Mr. Hazen what the feeling of the Canadian Government was towards obtaining Kelly's release, that if they were still anxious to have if brought about they would take further action.	'
I answered Mr. McCloskey saying that if I received a letter from the Embassy at Washington I would reply at once and would give them my own personal views very strongly. I said that the Canadian Government was anxious for Kelly's release and in no way lukewarm on the subject. I added * I am telling my secretary to-day to ascertain from the Justice Department and the Secretary of State if any matter has been sent from Ottawa to Mr. Bryce.'
I have gone somewhat at length into that because I thought I would like the House to know the facts, in view of the inference, and practically, I believe, the assertion, contained in the speech of the hon. member for Carleton to the effect that in this matter those who were not of his own political faith and who had been endeavouring to get Kelly's release were being actuated simply by political considerations. As far as I am concerned I want to disavow any such intention from start' to finish. The touching letter that was sent to me by Father Murphy in 'November, 1909, aroused	my	pity,	as	it would	havearoused	the	pity	of	any man	who
109i
possessed the slightest feeling of human sympathy. From that moment down to the present hour I have felt interested in the case. I have felt that a great hardship has been done and that the punishment imposed waS altogether in excess of what the crime imputed to this man deserved. I felt further that, if Kelly had been induced into the United States, even if he was not arrested on the Canadian side and dragged in, it was a most reprehensible proceeding and that, in addition, the long period which had elapsed since the offence charged against him had occurred, made the sentence of ten years imposed by the judge for that offence a sentence which was thoroughly and absolutely in excess of what the justice of the case demanded and that the imposition of a further penalty of four years was little less than an outrage and something that the courts of the United States should not regard with pride in view of the sentences which they impose for such offences throughout the country. On the 3rd December, 1910, I communicated to Sir Allen Aylesworth the facts of the case in consequence of the representations made to me by Father Murphy. 1 did not know Father Murphy. I did not know whether Father Murphy or whether Kelly was a Conservative or Liberal. I never asked anybody what their politics were and I did not care. If it had been represented to me that Kelly was the strongest Liberal to be found in New Brunswick, having some little feeling of decency and humanity, I would have exerted myself just as strongly to secure his freedom as I would if I had known him to have been a Conservative. I doubt if there is an hon. gentleman in this House, realizing the responsibility, I care not on 'what side of the House he is, who would for one moment have stopped to ask the question in a matter of this sort as to what the political faith or the political principles of this man might be on whose behalf he was asked to interest himself. He would only regard him as a citizen of Canada who had been unfairly and unjustly treated and from that standpoint, and that standpoint alone, he would exert himself and do all he could for him irrespective ef what his politics might be.
My hon. friend has gone out of his way- and one would almost think that that was the object of his bringing this matter before the House-to make an attack upon the Premier of New Brunswick by intimating that that gentleman took advantage of the death of Mrs. Kelly and the sad circumstances surrounding that

event to make political capital on the eve of the elections which occurred on the 20th June, 1912. I think, in view of the documents read by my hon. friend the Minister of Justice and the explanations he gave of these telegrams, that the hon.' member for Carleton must now be'assured that he was not justified in making this attack upon the Premier of New Brunswick, an attack which was unwarranted and which my hon. friend will recognize himself was made without sufficient justification.
What was th * charge that the hon. member for Carleton made against the Premier [DOT]of New Brunswick? The general local elections in New Brunswick were held on the 20th June, 1912. Mr. Flemming, the Premier, was, as he always had been, during his political career, a candidate for re-election in Carleton county with two other gentlemen on the ticket, the constituency re- . turning three members. Shortly before the election, it would appear from the correspondence, Mrs. Kelly was (Seized with what proved to be her last illness. Relatives and friends of Mrs. Kelly went to the Premier, who was the nearest member of the Government available and who was residing in the county not f-ar from where Mrs. Kelly lived, and asked him if he would not make a last effort so that Kelly might get out of the penitentiary and return to his home before his wife passed away. I care not whether an election is being held or not, is there a man in Canada who would refuse an appeal of that sort? The Premier of New Brunswick did just what my lion, friend would have done, just what I would have done, or what any other man in this House would have done. He addressed the following telegraphic communication on the 10th June to thq Secretary of State at Ottawa:
William Kelly, of Richmond, N.B., was convicted about two years ago for assault on a customs officer and for smuggling and sentenced to Atlanta, Ga„ prison for 14 years. There have been serious doubts whether he was arrested in the United States it being strongly claimed that he was on British soil when arrested. His wife is now seriously ill with an incurable disease and will probably not live more than a month. He has nine helpless children. Will you not make an earnest appeal on his behalf? Humanity calls for his being allowed to see his wife before she dies; feeling very strong that he should be liberated on ticket-of-leave; kindly appeal to President Taft if necessary.
(Sgd) J. K. Flemming, Premier New Brunswick.
That telegram was received in Ottawa on the llt-h instant, and Mr. Flemming was sent the following reply by the Under Secretary of State, Mr. Thomas MuJvey:

Your telegram respecting case of William Kelly received and transmitted to Governor General for action.
On June 11 Mr. Mulvey sent this communication, which I should judge to be a letter and not a telegram, to Mr. Flemming:
I have the honour to acknowledge the receipt to-day of your telegram of the 16th instant.
Then the telegram is given in full and the letter concludes:
This message has been communicated to the Governor General's office, in order that His Royal Highness, may, if he deems it proper to do so, transmit it to the Hon. Mr. Bryce, British Ambassador at Washington.
On the 15th June this telegram was received at the Governor General's office:
Washington, D.C., June 15, 1912.
Referring to your telegram, 11th June United States must be informed where Kelly will go if released on ticket-of-leave. Is his wife at Richmond? Telegraph reply with least possible delay to Percy, 26 East Erie street, Chicago.
(Sgd) Innes.
That is the signature of Mr. Mitchell Innes who was the principal official in [DOT]the British Embassy during the time that the Hon. James Bryce was British Ambassador. Having received that, Mr. Pelletier, an official in the Department of the Secretary of State, on the 17th June, three days before the election, wires this to Mr. Flemming:
Hon. J. K. Flemming,
Premier of New Brunswick,
Hartland, N.B.
Referring to your telegram of 10th of June instant re application for release of William Kelly of Richmond, N.B., United States Government must be informed where Kelly will go if released on ticket-of-leave and also if his wife is at Richmond; answer immediately.
On the I8th Mr. Flemming wired from Harland, N.B., to Mr. Pelletier, Acting Under Secretary of State, Ottawa:
Telegram received. William Kelly's wife died yesterday, nine children without any one to care for them, Kelly would no doubt desire to come home to Richmond, N. B., if released.
J. K. Flemming.
That is the whole correspondence with regard to this matter, so far as 1 can see. I think that if I had received that telegram from Mr. Mitchell Innes of the Ambassador's office, asking to be informed where Kelly would go if released, I would have felt buoyed up with the hope that the question was being asked because it was the intention of the United States authorities to release him forthwith. I do not for a moment hesitate to say that, and

I submit to the judgment of hon. gentlemen in that regard.
That telegram was received by Mr. Flemming, and the charge which my hon. friend (Mr. Carvell) makes is, that on the day of the funeral of Mrs. Kelly-I presume it was the day before the election, or the day of the election, because she died on the 17th, a telegram was received at the grave announcing that Kelly had been released and was on his way home.
I see from the correspondence; the telegram from Mr. Flemming is dated on the 18th, and he says she died last evening, so that the funeral would not be earlier than the 19th or 20th-Mr. Flemming no doubt communicated, as it was his duty to do, to those friends who had been "urging Kelly's release, a copy of the telegram received from Mr. Mitchell Innes at Washington, and they may have come to the conclusion, and I would not blame them for doing so, that it meant that Kelly was going to be released. My hon. friend (Mr. Carvell) has referred to the impression which a lady, no doubt acting in good faith, who was present at the funeral, gave as to what she understood the telegram to contain, but I would not be a bit surprised, and I think the fact is, that the telegram referred to was the one from Mr. Mitchell Innes to Premier Flemming, and from the fact that it is asked, in the- event of his being released, to what place he would be returned, they jumped to the conclusion that negotiations had proceeded so far that the American Government had decided to discharge him.
I know Mr. Flemming probably as well as any man knows him. He was an associate of mine, and was my right-hand man in the House of Assembly for twelve years. We sat together in opposition, and we sat together as members of the same government, and knowing Mr. Flemming as I do I have no hesitation in saying that he would under no possible circumstances, whether he needed votes-and he did not need them much at that election, judging by the result-or whether he did not, be guilty of the act insinuated against him by the hon. member (Mr. Carvell). Under no circumstances would Mr. Flemming, nor would any other man with the slightest sense of decency or respectability endeavour to make political capital out of so sad an event as the death of Mrs. Kelly, and out of the circumstances of her husband being confined in a penitentiary in the States. The idea that-when friends were assembled at them, when the Angel
of Death was hovering over a household, when the people were wrapped in grief and mourning-that any man with any sense of decency would resort to a trick of that sort, is beyond comprehension. Knowing Mr. Flemming as I do, I unhesitatingly say that he never would be a party to a proceeding of that sort. Mr. Flemming in making that request to the Department of the Secretary of State acted as any one else would under the circumstances, and in addition to that he no doubt handed to the relatives of Mrs. Kelly the telegram that had been received by him from Ottawa, and which had been sent first to the State Department at Ottawa and then forwarded to Mr. Flemming. From that telegram, they would without doubt have reasonably buoyed themselves up with the hope that a decision had been come to and that Kelly was going to be released. Perhaps I have taken up the time of the House at too great length.

Would my hon. friend
give the date of the telegram from Mr. Mitchell Innes?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The telegram from Mr. Mitchell Innes to the Governor General's secretary is dated the 15th of June; the telegram from the State Department here to Mr. Flemming is dated 17th June, and it was on the 18th of June that Mr. Flemming telegraphed back to the acting Secretary of State, Mr. Pelletier, telling him Mr. Kelly's wife had died the previous day, which would be the 17th, the day that telegram, which had been received by the Governor General, was sent out from the Secretary of State's Department. Perhaps I have trespassed too long upon the attention of the House, but it is a serious question and a most serious charge has been made by the hon. member (Mr. Carvell). I thought it was only right to give the full particulars to him. I can say that from the time I was first approached by Father Murphy of Debec in 1909 down to the present hour, the thought of making any political capital out of this event has never once entered my mind. I would like further to say, that I still believe, as strongly as I have felt all through, that a very great hardship has been done to Kelly. I do not attempt to excuse him for smuggling, but admitting he did the worst that is charged against him, he has done nothing under all the circumstances which, to my mind, as I said before would justify such a punishment as has been meted out to him. And, while everything possible has been done by the Depart-

ment of Justice under both Governments to bring about his release and his restoration to his nine unfortunate children, deprived of a mother's tender care in their childhood, we still have the fact that Kelly has been in the penitentiary for a period of nearly four years. Perhaps, a strong appeal might now be made-I am sorry it was not made along the lines I suggested a year ago-on the ground of humanity and on the ground of mercy, to have the man released from the penitentiary before his sentence has expired.
I do not think there is any more to be gained by presenting arguments on the grounds already advanced. Apparently, everything has been done in that direction that could be done, but something might be done emanating perhaps from the province of New Brunswick and the citizens of New Brunswick, by means of the presentation of a petition to the President of the United States, and by strong urging of this petition, to have the sentence passed on this unfortunate man commuted. If I can contribute anything to that by my personal service, as I said in the letter I wrote, by even going to Washington personally to see the President, or the other proper authority, I will only be too glad to do so, and in doing so I would not feel that I was doing any more than one man should do for another, in the interests of our common humanity.

It is somewhat surprising to learn that a member occupying a seat in this House has not the right to make a plain statement of fact, such as I did this afternoon, without being charged by the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Marine with having made an attack on a man who is not here to defend himself. I supposed that every member of this House had an absolute right to state facts. If the only argument that can be adduced from these facts implies underhand methods, so much the worse for the men who made that possible, and if the Minister of Marine can read from these facts, as he said himself : 'No man with the slightest sense of decency would state such a thing,' and if he can apply that to his friend Mr. Flemming, then I am sorry for Mr. Flemming. But after all the castigation of the Minister of Marine and the Minister of Justice, I have not a word to withdraw. On the contrary, if I would do what I ought to do here, I would read to the Minister of Marine some editorials and some correspondence which 
appeared in his newspaper, the St. John Standard, within the five or six days prior to the election of 1911, and perhaps the Minister of Marine would then be able to appreciate the standpoint from which I view this, as well as from his own broad humanitarian standpoint. I did not charge the Minister of Marine with being guilty of any underhand or unfair tactics. He was only the method or the means by which the other fellows did it. When my hon. friend harps back to 1909 and tells this House what he did after receiving a letter from Father Murphy, he only did what any man would have done under the circumstances; he did only what it was his duty as Attorney General of New Brunswick to do. I give him neither credit' nor blame. I would have blamed him if he had done less, and I do not know that I would have asked him to do more. He set the machinery in operation; he corresponded with the Department of Justice. I can tell him how his letter got into the hands of the Minister of Justice. It was handed to me by Father Murphy, and I handed it to the Minister of Justice. I have tried to give the House and the department all the information I possibly could.
Knowing what I do about what took place in the election of 1911, knowing all the charges of perfidy that were made against me by a man whose name has been drawn in here-and before I am through I will have something to say about this Dr. Kirkpatrick, the man who had been my political friend, whom I had recommended and succeeded in having appointed to office, the man who turned traitor for a consideration, the man who became the partner of B. F. Smith afterwards, the man who with B. F. Smith organized the West India Trading Company, about which my hon. friend knows something, the man who robbed the farmers of the county of Carle-ton of about $15,000 and who had to flee the country. This is the man who wrote the article in the Standard and who carried the telegram of Mr. Flemming to that woman's grave and had it read there in the presence of her relatives and friends. After what had taken place in the election of 1911, it was pretty hard to do less than they did, because I find a letter from Mr. Smith's friend, Dr. Kirkpatrick, asking the minister to' do something. That was in January, and the whole matter ceased and not a finger was lifted before the local election in June, six months afterwards. Then my friends got busy again. Then Mr. MARCH 16, 1914
B. F. Smith thought it an outrage that Mr. Kelly should be left in prison. Then Mr. Flemming sent a telegram to the minister, and the correspondence took place which we have heard read to-night from my hon. friend's private file. I want to know if it happened only as an incident, if it was only an accident that Mr. Flemming got that telegram on the 17th day of June?

My hon. friend cannot
draw me away from what I have in my mind; I will get through with it. Mr. Flemming got that telegram on the 17th day of June. speechtext: I do not know whether it * was the document or not.

I know there was what purported to be a telegram from Ottawa, addressed to the Hon. J. K. Flemming, read at that woman's grave. My hon. friend says that it was the telegram sent to him on the 17th day of June. If it was not that telegram, it was manufactured. If we can believe the story of this lady, whom everybody in Carleton county will believe, I have very grave doubts if it was the telegram. But if it was, it is a most amazing thing that Mr. Flemming and his friends could keep that telegram in their possession for two days and then time the thing so perfectly that this same Dr. Kirkpatrick could arrive at the village of Debec just when the funeral procession was being formed, could have handed the telegram to the chief henchmen of the parish and [DOT]	9 p.m. have bad it read at the graveside in the presence of tho.se people. It is a most wonderful coincidence. I think my hon. friend had better have saved his friend the Premier of New_ Brunswick from the humiliation of having the facts laid bare before the people. I made no charge .against the Premier of New Brunswick; I simply laid bare the facts. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice accuses me of saying something behind Mr. Flemming's back that I would not say to his face." I do not think Mr. Flemming will ever charge me with going behind his back or with refusing to say' to his face anything that I have to say to him. I do not think I have that reputation anywhere in the province of New Brunswick. I usually say to people's faces what I have to say to them.
I wish to discuss the other branch of the case just for a moment, because we must remember that since October 12 this matter has been a dead letter. The department have, taken it for granted that no case can be made out for Kelly, and that Kelly must stay out his term in jail unless the United States Government see fit in the goodness of their heart to release him. My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has touched upon an argument which I put forward on many occasions to the late Minister of Justice, and I almost think it will be found in the correspondence. If not, however, it was certainly used by me. The argument which I always thought should be put up to the United States Government is this question: Can a friendly civilized nation afford to allow its officials to go into the territory of another civilized nation and by deceit or trickery inveigle a citizen of that civilized nation into their territory in order to apprehend him for a crime, no matter how heinous it may be ? I have never believed that the United States officials were justified under international comity, if not under international law, to proceed in that way. If this Government will put up the argument to the United States Government whether they feel that they are justified in sending their officials over to the Dominion of Canada, there by bribery and cajolery to induce one of our citizens to cross over into their territory in order to liiive him arrested, I think the United States Government would listen to such an argument. Of course, I do not admit for a moment that Kelly voluntarily crossed the boundary line. I do not believe that he did so. I believe that if they would send a responsible commissioner to the county of Carleton, or to that vicinity, he would have very grave doubts as to whether this man voluntarily went into the United States. I am amazed to learn that the British consul at Washington came up there to investigate matters, because, if he did, he took very great pains not to let anybody on our side of the line know that he was coming there. If this be the way in which the British officials look after our interests, the sooner that the Can-

adian Government look after our interests in international matters the better. Perhaps I am now travelling outside the realm of this discussion, but that view has been forced upon me this afternoon and evening in a manner in which I have never looked at it before. To think of the British consul coming to investigate the question of the freedom of a British subject, taking the evidence of American officials, taking the evidence only of the men who were interested in maintaining one side of the discussion and absolutely ignoring the parties themselves who were most vitally interested in this matter, is a condition of affairs which I can hardly conceive, although it must be true, because we have it in the return and the name of the offi-'cial who came here. Let that be as it will, I still believe that, if a commissioner were appointed, came to that country, took the evidence of both sides, allowing both sides to be represented by counsel, and got down to the very bottom of the matter, he would be able to shake the faith of the United States Government in the story told by their officials. But above and beyond all other questions is the broad question, as I have said, whether the United States Government can afford to stand before the world as being the means of sending their officials to our country to bribe and trap and inveigle our citizens to their country in order that they may aTrest and prosecute them for offences committed years before. I hope the Minister of Justice will take note of what has been said by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and by myself, and that one more attempt will be made to release William Kelly. If nothing more has been accomplished by the discussion to-night, I trust we shall at least have taken this matter out of politics never to return. It has played too great a part among Tory politicians in the province of New Brunswick within the last four or five years. I hope that is ended, and in future this unfortunate man and his family will be treated as British subjects, as human beings, and not as the football for certain politicians.
Motion agreed to.	.

subtopic: INTERCOLONIAL RAILWAY-THE CASE OF AMASA E. KILLAM.
speechtext:
This is not a very contentious matter. In moving it, I wish to

bring to .the attention of the Government a condition of things relating to this gentleman, and to a number of others, in connection with the Provident Fund Act, which, I think, calls for consideration by the Administration, and particularly by the Department of Railways. Mr. Killam, the gentleman named in the resolution, was appointed early in 1897 as inspector of bridges and buildings on the Intercolonial railway. He occupied that position with credit, I am sure, to himself, and with advantage to the railway and the country. He attended closely to the duties of his position, I think to the satisfaction of all concerned. Mr. Killam had been for many yeaTs a bridge-builder of great and good repute, a man with probably the greatest experience in bridge building of any man in the province of New Brunswick. He stood high in the estimation of the people of his native county of Westmorland, so much so that on more than one occasion he was elected to represent them in the legislature of that province. Indeed, at the time of his appointment he was a membeT of the legislature representing the county of Westmorland. His fitness for the position led to the then Minister of Railways, the late Hon. Mr. Blair, tendering him the appointment to this office which was vacant. Mr. Killam was appointed, and served, I think, down to August last. His duties required him to travel over the whole length of the Intercolonial railway, because he had jurisdiction over all the bridges from 8te. Rosalie to Halifax and from Truro to Sydney, and on the branches of the railway also. In August, or at some other time in 1913, his services were dispensed with, for what reason I know not, nor is it material. I am sure there was no dissatisfaction with the way in which he performed his duties. For it was from some other cause, reorganization or whatever it may have been, that his services were dispensed with. It was within the knowledge of this House that on the 1st of April, 1907, there came into force an Act known as the Intercolonial and Prince Edward Island Railway Employees' Provident Fund Act which provided that every employee of the Intercolonial, of date April 1, would be entitled to participate in the provisions of the Act, whereby a fund was provided which would be a safeguard and .a protection to them when they had. severed their connection with the railway, according to the provisions of the Act. I need not refer at length to the provisions of the Act. Section 12 provides:
The following classes of persons shall, upon the recommendation of the hoard and the approval of the minister, subject to this Act and to the rules and regulations of the board, upon being retired by the minister from service, be entitled, for the remainder of their lives, to monthly allowances as provided for in this Act.
Then it goes on to recite the different classes of employees-a, b, c, d; and then we had class e:
Those who, previous to the coming into force of this Act, entered the service at such an advanced age as to cause them to reach the age of seventy years before being fifteen years in the service, provided that on attaining the age of seventy years they have been at least ten years in the service.
A question has arisen as to whether Mr. Killam is entitled to participate in the benefits of this Act. It will be borne in mind that he joined the service in 1897. Mr. Killam claimed that he was engaged as such bridge and building inspector in March, 1897, and that his engagement, made in that month, was with the Minister of Railways, then the late Hon. Mr. Blair. Mr. Killam reached the age of seventy in 1906. Mr. Killam claims that he was an employee engaged' April 1, 1897, and that he had served ten years previous to the date when he reached the age of seventy years. It appears that the Provident Fund Board claim that he was one month short of having served ten years previous to reaching the age of seventy years. Mr. Killam states that there is evidence in the department corroborating the fact that he was employed on April 1, 1896. The manager of the Intercolonial railway in dispensing with his -services, claimed that he was one month short and therein lies the contention between Mr. Killam and the railway. Under this Act, every employee of date April 1, 1907, participates in its benefits and should pay monthly into the fund established by the Act a certain percentage of his wages or salary. This was done in the ease of Mr. Killam, as it was done in the case of every other employee; and down to the month when his services were dispensed with he paid into that fund a certain percentage of his salary, which wa3 $150 a month, that is at the rate of $1,800 a year. The position of the department in relation to Mr. Killam s claim is purely technical; it certainly is not equitable. At any rate if they had a record of his age and of the date when he

would have reached seventy years, if the Act is to be strictly observed, when an employee reaches seventy years his payments cease and it would be the duty of the Secretary of the Provident Fund Board to cut off the exaction, of his monthly contributions to that fund as soon as he reaches the age of seventy years. After he had reached that age he was still called upon to contribute to the fund, and continued to do so as long as he was employed by the Government. When 'his services were dispensed with, naturally supposing that he would be entitled to the retiring allowance provided for under the Act, he made a claim for it, but his claim has not been recognized. I had hoped that the matter could have been discussed when the Minister of Railways was in the House. Naturally he is more familiar with the working of the Act and probably has cognizance of this particular case. I had hoped to bring it to his attention publicly in the House-I have already spoken to him about it privately-in order that he might make provision for the payment of this retiring 'allowance even though there might be some technical objection against it. I have not, however, been able to claim the attention of the Minister of Railways who is unfortunately absent through illness, and as this is the last day on which I can present the case it is my desire to emphasize the ifaets to the acting Minister of Railways in the hope that he will be able to deal with the case and do justice to the claim of Mr. Kjllani. The fact that his services were dispensed with after he had passed the age of seventy in no way affects the ease. But even if the law is strictly interpreted and rigidly applied, yet the Minister of Railways in a meritorious case could arrange for this man to get his retiring allowance. Let me explain. The length of service may be either the actual service or the actual length of service with an addition by the Government. If the contention of the Department of Railways is correct, Mr. Killam would be short in the service just one month of the time when he would be entitled to the retiring allowance. It has been usual in all the departments at Ottawa, and in the case of the Intercolonial railway at Moncton, to extend the period of service in cases of retirement. We all know that judges of the Supreme Court and county courts are emitted to retire and receive an allowance by adding to the term of their service, which action is taken by the Treasury Board. The same thing applies to the Intercolonial railway. I have in my mind 
the case of Mr. J. J. Wallace, whose term of service was added to. That was some few years ago. Mr. Wallace had been in the employ of the Intercolonial railway for many years. His first employment dated back to the eighties and perhaps earlier. Exception was made in his case; also in the case of Mr. Tiffin who occupied the position of general traffic manager of the Intercolonial railway. He was transferred to Toronto at a lower salary. He continued at the same salary for a certain period and there are other cases which I could give my hon. friend the acting Minister of Railways. In many instances parties retiring from the service are allowed three, four or six months ahead. In one particular instance an allowance of a year was made. In this particular case, we have a gentleman occupying a high position in the confidence of his fellow^men, and who is recognized as having been a very faithful servant of the public for many years, and it seems to me that bis case is certainly entitled to all the consideration that the department can give it. It is said that Mr. Killam's services were dispensed with because he had attained the age of seventy in 1906, and that he was, therefore, seventy-six or seventy-seven when he retired. Whatever his age in years, no one who knows his robust physique, his strong mentality, his activity in the discharge of his duties, will say that he was incapacitated in any degree because of his years.
Mr. Killam to-day, active, hale, hearty, physically and mentally, is as capable of the performance and discharge of his duties as he was fifteen or twenty years ago. This may possibly be an extravagant statement, but it will he confirmed by all those who have knowledge of hiin. He discharged the duties of that position with satisfaction to the railway authorities and in the interest of the railway itself. By whom are those duties discharged to-day? By a civil engineer and an assistant engineer, both of whom have a staff of assistants. Mr. Killam did the work alone and single-handed. If age is to be a bar, if he is to be removed from the service because of his age, and if the Intercolonial railway are going upon that principle, I wonder why it is that They should bring from Nova Scotia as a consulting engineer in respect to bridges and all other matters, a gentleman who is upwards of 83 years of age.	.
