Martin Murphy, and. my hon. friend (Mr. Hazen) will know something of his age. For many years he had been provincial engineer in the province of Nova Scotia. He was retired on a pension in that province; an Act was passed recognizing his services and granting him a pension of $2,000 a year. He is today in the enjoyment of that pension. As a matter of fact, it has been stated that Mr. Killam's services were dispensed with because of age. If he should be discharged by reason of his age, upon what principle can the management turn around and employ a gentleman-and I have not anything to say against Mr. Murphy-who is to my knowledge upwards of 83? I have been told that he is nearer 87 than 83. He was brought there just about the time Mr. Killam's connection with the railway was severed. But that is not material to the question to which I would invite the attention of the acting Minister of Railways and Canals. Now there is the case of Mr. Killam. There are several other cases. I .am familiar with two or three people who have been for a number of years employed on the railway, the circumstances of whose employment are entirely similar to those of Mr. Killam's. There is the case of Mr. J. B. Tingley, the case of Mr. Isaac Hicks, the case of Mr. Sears and perhaps one or two others. There are some six cases that stand exactly in the same position. These persons were in the employment of the Intercolonial railway on the 1st April, 1897, and they had been continued in the employment of that railway down to within the last few months. The services of Mr. Tingley, of Mr. Hicks and the others were dispensed with but a few months ago. Although they have contributed to this fund and anticipated that they would be entitled to retire with all the benefits and -advantages accruing out of the fund, they have been retired and the benefits have been denied to them. The railway may be justified in refusing, under the law, and I am not sufficiently familiar with the facts to allow me to pass judgment upon that, but, be that as it may, I think they are cases that should receive the equitable consideration of the Railway Department by reason of the long and faithful services of these men, by reason of the fact that they have contributed, and by reason of the further fact that they have made these contributions under the impression that they would be entitled
to the receipt of a retiring allowance. The Act is explicit and I think that in this particular case, as indeed, in the other cases, the department will be justified in extending the length of service for the short period of one month at least, thereby enabling them under the law to receive the benefits which are provided under this Act. I suppose that any one of us holding a position, and with the years creeping upon us, would naturally be shocked at being summarily dismissed from the service of the railway. I do not know, I am sure, that any charges were brought against Mr. Killam. It is true that he was a Liberal. My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) knows that, but certainly the law was enacted for the benefit of all shades of political faith. When that law was passed in 1907, it was in contemplation that the ones who would receive the first benefits were those who were not ini sympathy with the Government that enacted the legislation and took the responsibility of it. The large proportion of the men to retire under the provisions of that Act were not those of the Liberal faith in politics. It is natural that those who had been the longest in the service were those who had been appointed by Conservative Governments. Presumably they were appointed because they were friends of Conservative Governments. That was the practice and let us not be hypocritical about it. The same practice was pursued by the Liberal Administration when they had appointments to make. Mr. Killam, Mr. Hicks, Mr. Tingley and the others whom I have named-and perhaps still others whose names I have not given because they do not occur to me at the moment-were appointees of the Liberal Administration. That certainly would not be recognized by this Administration even as a bar to their receipt of a fair and decent allowance under the provisions of the Act, providing they could come under the provisions of the Act.

Mr. Killam's place was not filled by promotion; tne gentleman who is discharging the duties formerly discharged by him had no connection with the Intercolonial previously, and did not even come from the Maritime provinces. I have no reflection at all to cast upon that gentleman, but I do ask that Mr. Killam shall receive full consideration. I have moved for these papers in order that I might present to the Department of Railways the merits of Mr. Killam's claim, and I trust the acting minister will see that full justice be done him.	*

He is in the service of the railway and necessarily, as an engineer, he is called upon to do active' work. But my hon. friend says it is necessary to have the bridges strengthened. He thereby displayed his ignorance with respect to the Intercolonial railway. I wish to tell him that the bridges on the Intercolonial railway have been strengthened to enable them to carry the heaviest engines. True, there is one small portion of the road where that work has not been completed, and that is in Cape Breton. But on the'main line of the Intercolonial railway, from Ste. Rosalie clear through to Halifax, the bridges have been renewed and strengthened. And if he visits the Intercolonial railway, at Boundary Creek and at other places along the line, he will find the old bridges that were taken from the Intercolonial railway piled up. He seems to think that it would not be possible in any way to interfere with this because there would be some disturbance in connection with the employees. He himself is the party who is every day doing the very thing that is disturbing -the equilibrium of this Provident Fund Act. That Act says that among those who can participate in the benefits of the Act are:
Class C. Those who have attained the age of sixty years after being fifteen years in the service, and request to be retired from the service.
They cannot be removed from their positions, except for cause, and they cannot be given a retiring allowance until the request has been made by them to be retired. But, during the last six months the Intercolonial railway officials have been working overtime removing men from office in order to replace them with adherents of the Conservative party. When my hon. friend takes his ground in answer to a simple request made by me, I would call his attention to some wholesome truths with respect to the ' disturbance of the equilibrium of the Provident Fund Act,' which disturbance is greatly to the injury of the employees of the railway and to the damage of the younger generation who are called upon to make good the losses which result from this dismissing of men without cause and without any charge made against them. Letters are written to these men: You had better retire; make your request to retire under the Provident Fund Act. These letters do

not say in so many words: If you do not make your request we will dismiss you,- but they coerce the employees into asking for retirement under the Act. I can cite dozens of cases within my own knowledge. And yet, because I ask that consideration shall be given to this particular ease, my hon. friend says, that I am responsible. It is true, no provision was made with respect to this matter. I should have protected those who were appointed, because I might have known that those who would suffer would be my own political friends. In so far as I showed lack of foresight, I acknowledge my mistake. But I certainly did not contemplate that ever an administration would come into power that would ruthlessly trample upon or ignore the provisions of the Act, and the rights of the employees of the railway and their claims as men. I dealt with the matter on the basis of even-handed justice, and while I was there even-handed justice was dealt out. When I was Minister of Railways, and afterwards when that office was filled by my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham), in the administration of this Act it made no difference whether a man was a Liberal or a Conservative; and there are hundreds to-day who retired under the Liberal Administration, men who were Conservatives in politics and whose declining years are safeguarded and protected by the operation of this Act. Yet, because I ask that the acting minister should give personal consideration to the merits of this case, he enters into a partisan controversy. I am sorry the Minister of Railways (Mr. Cochrane) is not here. I think he wrote a letter with respect to this very case, stating that if it were necessary in order to do justice, he would have an amendment made to the Act. If injustice was done by reason of my want of foresight in the framing of the Act, it is open to my hon. friend now, during this very session, to make a simple amendment to provide that justice shall be done where injustice is now being done. I had some hopes that the Minister of Railways, had he been here, would have treated this matter from the standpoint of one desirous of dealing justly with the employees of the Intercolonial railway. But I lose hope in connection with this case as long as it is under the control of the acting minister, after the exhibition he has made of his animus in this particular case and in other cases to which I have called attention.

For a copy of all correspondence, documents, recommendations and reports, respecting the dredging of Des Prairies) river, the work' done, depth, length and width of channel dredged, the list of men employed to perform that work, their salaries respectively, and the amount of money spent on that work since the 22nd of November, 1912, up to the 2nd of February, 1914.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am delighted that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) is in his seat. If he will refer to the debates of this House as far back as 1908 or 1909, he will find that, at my request and with the approval of one of his friends then sitting near me, the Hon. Mr. Monk, certain sums of money were put in the Estimates for the dredging of Des Prairies river. At that time the question of the Georgian Bay canal was a live topic and, according to the very valuable report of four engineers appointed by this Government, there was a question as to whether the Georgian Bay canal should enter the St. Lawrence by the southern route, via Ste. Anne, or by another route north of the island of Montreal, known as the alternative route. My contention was that, even without reference to that grand canal project, any money spent for dredging the river Des Prairies would be well spent, if only for the purpose of improving navigation in that river, while the improvement wouild, of course, be useful when the Georgian Bay canal project became an actuality. I was listened to, and I think very properly, and an amount of 860,000 was put in the Estimates of 1909 and of 1910 and of 1911. I do not mean that an amount of $60,000 was put in the Estimates each of these years and spent. Everybody knows what the Des Prairies river is. It is about thirty-two miles long. It runs from Bout de L'Isle, below the island of Montreal, to the lake of Two Mountains, and if you follow the southern shore of lake of Two Mountains you reach Ste. Anne and Vaudreuil. We need improvements on that river. The population living

on the shore is very large. It was not very numerous fifteen or twenty years ago, but now the city of Montreal has increased so that there are no less than two wards on the 'river, Ahunt-sic ward and Bordeaux ward. I am delighted to see the Secretary of State (Mr. Coderre) in his seat. He knows that where there were only farms a few years ago there are now thriving towns. We have many institutions on the shores of that river. One of them is rather an ancient one, having existed since Confederation-the penitentiary of St. Vincent de Paul. The population there is now five hundred, and the Government are spending about $150,000 a year for the support of the institution. The consumption of one article, coal, varies between $3,000 and $5,000 a year. The transportation of coal to that institution is most expensive. According to the reports in the Department of Justice from the inspectors of prisons, to mention only two, Mr. Douglas Stewart and Mr.	Dawson, it will
be seen that they have calculated that at the penitentiary at St. Vincent de Paul the Government could save a $1 a ton on the transportation of coal, which would come to between $1,000 and $2,000 a year. That would be a good investment even if we spend $50,000 or $100,000 just to dredge that river. This is no new scheme. In 1865, when the old convent of the Sacred Heart was transformed into a reform prison to start with and then into a penitentiary, convicts were brought down to St. Vincent de Paul at high water in the spring by a boat named the Eagle. There was a wharf there. The wharf has been destroyed, and I am now asking for the restoration of navigation. I understand that transportation was one of the difficulties in that period; but to-day building materials of every kind -nstone, wood, lumber, shingles, and cement -can be transported from Montreal and at a much cheaper rate than we could transport them then. I was delighted to see in the Estimates for 1911 the sum of $25,000; it was rather small, but on this side we are happy when we can get even a little piece of those Estimates. Every year since 1911, $25,000 has been set aside for dredging, but we have no dredge. We have dredge No. 6, a special one, and I feel certain that we have dredged right across the St. Lawrence from the main channel and under the Canadian Northern railway bridge as far as Rivi&re des Prairies a good channel eight feet deep at low water and 100 feet wide. It allows to come up scows with a [Mr. C. A. Wilson '
draught of five or six feet and tugs drawing six or seven feet. I cannot see why this sum of $25,000 which appears in the Estimates each year has not been wiped out. The dredge has now reached a point below St. Vincent de Paul. I urge my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works to get some information on this point from the Minister of Inland Revenue or the Secretary of State, who are very familiar with the case. I am sorry that the late member for Jacques Cartier is not here to deal with this question, as he could do it much more eloquently than I. The dredge could proceed right up to the lake of Two Mountains, for the benefit of residents of Riviere des Prairies, St. Vincent de Paul, Bordeaux, and St. Martin Dorothea. We need navigation up there, and I hope my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works with his big heart will not only put $25,000 in the Estimates, but will . add to that the $25,000 of last year and the $25,000 of the year before, making $75,000, and I hope he will not merely have it printed on a sheet of paper by the King's Printer, but will see that dredge No. 6, which he will find behind St. Helen's island, gets to work. The mow is melting, the ice will soon be drifting down and the river will be clear, and now is the time to get the dredge in good working shape, and to get the tug under steam and painted-painted blue if you like, but get it to work anyway.
Does my hon. friend consider the dredging of Des Prairies as a separate undertaking, or as necessarily forming a part of the Georgian Bay canal scheme? It makes a lot of difference.

I do not think it makes any difference at all whether a shovelful of mud is taken out of a river for navigation at the present time or for the Georgian Bay canal scheme later on. I do not see Why when the Georgian Bay canal scheme comes into effect, if it ever does, it will be necessary to throw that shovelful of mud back again.

If my hon. friend refers to the plans made by the eminent engineers of the Government, Mr. Lafleur and others, he will find that the Georgian Bay canal is constructed at that part of the river by elevating the surface of the water by means of dams, one of them being situated at Bout de l'lle and the other in the neighbourhood of the projection of St. Denis street. I think it is very important to decide first whether or not this enterprise is to be a part of the Georgian Bay canal scheme, or whether it is simply a matter of the construction-of a channel eight

173J
to ten feet deep, although the latter would also be very useful, I admit, for navigation between Montreal and the Back River district.

Mr. Speaker, after listening to the remarks just made by the hon. member for Laval (Mr. Wilson), I may say that I agree heartily with him in the statements he has made. There is no finer prospect in the world than that part of the river Ottawa which extends from Bout de l'lle and passes by St. Vincent de Paul, Ahuntsic, Sault au Recollet, Cartierville, l'lle Bizard and St. Genevieve and then enters the lake of Two Mountains.
It is certainly the most beautiful stretch of the river Ottawa. Residents along the banks of that part of the river are many of them very influential people, rich property owners. The reasons set forth by the hon. member for Lavall are very cogent, but he has let slip one of them, Mr. Speaker, and to my mind, the most weighty: we are the owners at St. Vincent de Paul of 800 ar-pents of land, and I may assure you, sir, that should those improvements be carried out, the value of that property would be very materially increased.
Who is the owner?

My family owns it. It is the best reason I could urge, although possibly I had better not mention it, since the hon. gentleman is not likely to take much stock in considerations of that kind. And in the direction of Cartierville and St. Laurent we hold also large interests. But apart from any personal motives, improvements such as those projected are surely in order. It is a pity to see such a fine stream left in a state unsuitable for navigation. Such improvements would certainly enhance materially the value of every property bordering the river, whether situated on the island of Montreal or on the ile JAsus.
What is the average depth of the river des Prairies?
Seven feet on an average if the boulders referred to by me were removed.

Some parts of the river are very deep. Between the Sault au Recollet and the confluence of the Ottawa with the St. Lawrence, the depth at some places is sixty feet. You may be sure, sir, that if the Government wishes to spend to advantage public moneys, they cannot find a better place for effecting improvements.
There is some pretty heavy work to do at Moulin du Crochet; rapids to do away with. Those rapids are a little lower down than St. Vincent de Paul.
Once those improvements are carried out, a cruise along that river will afford the finest pleasure trip imaginable, between Bout de File and the lake of Two Mountains, and besides the land values would go up materially.
That would be more profitable than the pleasure trip.

Of course, when i speak of pleasure trips, I do not wish to dissociate business from pleasure. A new institution has been established on the banks of the river des Prairies, I mean the new Montreal gaol. As is generality known, large amounts have been expended on that building, and large quantities of materials and supplies are being constantly forwarded there. Were it possible to ship them by boat, a great saving would be effected. There are mills in operation in that vicinity and the establishment of others is forecasted.
As pointed out by the hon. gentleman from Nicolet (Mr. Lamarche), a still more pressing scheme is that for the building of the Georgian Bay canal. I visited that part of the country; I even went as far as Georgian bay, and I well satisfied myself as to the advantages which the citizens of Montreal, as well as residents on the banks of the river Ottawa, would reap through the building of that canal. All agree on that point; and you must have perceived with a great deal of pleasure, Mr. Speaker, that in Montreal particularly there is but one opinion on that point. Boards of trade, municipal corporations, all public bodies are unanimous in urging that this work be carried out as soon as possible.
We are in the habit of quarrelling about this and that and the other thing; but in regard to this matter there is only one opinion, and the country could not make too great sacrifices for the purpose of starting the work at the earliest possible date. All the same, let us not lose sight of St. Vincent de Paul and St. Laurent.

Mr. Speaker, first let me
say in reply to the hon. member for Montcalm (Mr. Lafortune) that the reasons which he advanced for the necessity of this work certainly appeal to me. To some extent, at all events, this work would be an advantage for the transportation of prisoners to the penitentiary at St. Vincent de Paul.



That would be a certain advantage to the country and the work would be deserving of consideration from that point of view. The additional reason which my hon. friend from Montcalm advanced, that he was the happy possessor, together with his family, of 700 acres of land which would be very much benefited by the construction of this work, which he thinks should be undertaken, is another reason which appeals to myself. Let me say to my hon. friend from Laval (Mr. Wilson) that there will not be the slightest objection to bringing down all the papers that his motion calls for. I quite agree with my hon. friend that this is not a new question and I might inform him that it has been pressed upon my attention, not only by those representing the construction of the Georgian Bay canal, but by others. In view of the fact that before the work of the Georgian Bay canal can be undertaken we must have the report of the commission that is about to be named to take into consideration the commercial feasibility of the enterprise, my hon. friend from Laval may not wish in connection with this local work, to wait for the report of that commission. However, as he has stated, it i3 no new question and I may say to him that it has been pressed from the local point of view upon my attention on two or three occasions by deputations from that locality. About a month ago a very strong deputation, headed by Mr. Leonard, presented very forcibly the necessity of the work which my hon. friend has spoken about to-night.
Not on that river?
Yes, the same one.
Well, you will hear from me on the motion which follows.

He was very anxious for this as for other works in connection with the river des Prairies. In reply to the hon. member for Nicolet (Mr. Lamarche), let me say that we must understand each other. The other night we agreed about the Georgian Bay canal and we still agree, but before the commencement of the work in the river des Prairies in 1909 Mr. Languedoc, an engineer of the Department of Public

Works, was asked to make a special survey, and, basing his figures upon the Georgian Bay canal report, he came to the conclusion that the work would cost $100,000, of which $15,000 could be applied to the construction of a lock at the rapide du Moulin du Crochet. My hon. friend the Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier), when he crosses the river going to Quebec, crosses the rapide du Moulin du Crochet. The lock at the rapide could be built for about $15,000, and then we would have a depth of seven or eight feet of water from Vercheres to Two Mountains.

The Georgian Bay
canal locks are designed to be 22 feet deep.

No, my hon. friend is
mistaken. The dredging from Vercheres straight from the river St. Lawrence channel, up through the rapide la Passe, the first rapid met on that river, will give us the depth of the locks of the Georgian Bay canal. The lock at the rapide la Passe will be 25 feet high, 650 feet long and about 60 feet wide. That is the first lock. There will here be a barrage extending out in the river, and the level of the river from that point will be raised 13 feet. You do not require any dredging from the rapide la Passe to the Sault au Recollet, because as a result of raising the water thirteen feet the rapid will be reduced to that extent and there will be no more Sault au Recollet rapid. If we do not start the Georgian Bay canal now, and if we start with the smaller scheme that I am speaking of, in order to have navigation between Bout de l'Isle and Two Mountains of seven or eight feet, all that is necessary is to dredge the rapide la Passe, build a lock at the Sault au Recollet, and dredge Whitehorse rapids and the rapide Lallemant.
To relieve the anxiety of my hon. friend (Mr. Lamarche) I may tell him that this is no promenade at all, but there are numbers of promenades on the St. Lawrence route. If the hon. gentleman will consult his good friend Sir Rodolphe Forget, the member for Montmorency, he .will find in the archives of the Richelieu and Ontario Navigation Company, that for fifteen years the steamer Terrebonne was carrying on a service from Montreal to Bout de l'lle, thence to Macdonald's wharf at L'Assomp-tion, and thence to St. Vincent de Paul, and back to Montreal. For fifteen years these wharfs were leased by the federal Government, and the steamer did a large traffic at them. The Minister of Public Works seems to have the idea that we need this

navigation for the transport of convicts to the St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary, but he is mistaken as to that. We used to get some convicts from Kingston, and a couple of years ago we got two carloads from Stony mountain, but that kind of interprovincial trade has now been stopped. The convicts at St. Vincent de Paul come mostly from the city of Montreal, and they are brought sometimes by boat but mostly by cabs. What the wharf is needed for mostly, is, for the coal and the general merchandise that is required at the penitentiary. The wharf would also be useful for the municipalities along the river, where there is considerable building going on, and quite a large trade.

That, in the opinion of this House, the time has arrived for the extension of the Intercolonial Railway of Canada into the non-railway sections of the Maritime provinces within reasonable range of the said railway?
He said: The subject of my resolution is of such importance that I must ask for a few minutes to place the more salient of the facts in connection with it before the House. I regret that I am obliged to bring this resolution forward when the Minister of Railways is not in his seat, and still more do I regret the cause of the absence of that hon. gentleman. I trust the time is not far distant when he will be able to be back to discharge his departmental and parliamentary duties. I do not profess to be able to enumerate the different sections of the Maritime provinces which require a further extension of railway facilities. No doubt the great province of Quebec, which we regard in Nova Scotia as a Maritime province, has now a great many railway facilities, but there are sections of the province which have no railway facilities, and which look forward with some hope to further extensions of the Intercolonial railway. What I say of the province of Quebec, no doubt applies with greater force to the province of New Brunswick and the province of Prince Edward Island.
But the observations I wish to address to the House to-night have more particular

reference to Nova Scotia, and more especially to the eastern part of that province. The western part of the province of Nova Scotia has from its earlier history better railway accommodation than we have in the far east. Particularly has this reference to the island of Cape Breton, one of the counties of which I have the honour to represent. The strait of Canso cutting off the important island of Cape Breton from the mainland made it for many years difficult for railways to be extended in the island, and even now we have some difficulty in having the better class of railway accommodation on the island because of the strait of Canso and by reason of the fact that that strait is crossed only by a boat instead of by a bridge.
The subject which I am now bringing to the attention o'f the House is not by any means a new one. In 1909, 1910, 1911, 1912, 1913 and now in 1914 I have brought this subject repeatedly before the attention of the House. Until something is done towards the advancement of railway accommodation, particularly in the county of Victoria which I have the honour to represent, I think it is my duty to continue bringing this matter to the notice of Parliament. It might perhaps be argued, as is argued sometimes, that we are fervent in regard to matters of expenditure of this character now that we are in opposition. So far as I am concerned, that argument cannot be applied for I was just as strenuous and just as diligent in bringing this matter to the notice of the House when I was supporting a government as I have been since the change of government took place.
I was much struck the other night in listening to the hon. member for Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles) place before this House the great claims the pioneers of the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Alberta, and,the claims of those western provinces. I do not for a moment- wish to belittle the claims of the pioneers of those provinces, but the pioneering there was never as strenuous or as difficult as the pioneering in the Maritime provinces, particularly in the province of Nova Scotia. I do not say that pioneering in that province was any more difficult than in the provinces of New Brunswick, Quebec or Ontario, because the character of the country that had to be dealt with in the province of Nova Scotia was mhch the same as that of the other provinces I have mentioned. Our forefathers in coming t-o Nova -Scotia had to

deal with huge forests covering the land right down to the water's edge. There were no roads, certainly no facilities of any kind except blazed trees along the rivers and lakes. Our forefathers in Nova Scotia, and particularly in the county of Victoria and North Cape Breton, which I have the honour to represent, hewed out for themselves homes in these woods and made a part of Canada which I am sure is entitled to as much recognition and consideration by any government that might be in power as any other part of the Dominion of Canada. When we talk about pioneering and what should be done to encourage pioneering, I submit to the Department of Railways and Canals and to the Prime Minister that the people of Nova Scotia who have settled on those shores some 100 or 150 years ago, and who are to-day something like 100 or 150 miles away from any railway, are entitled to the consideration of the Government and of this House.
When we live in a great country like Canada, a country that is pulsating with development from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and when we find that the interior of this vast land of ours is receiving the benefit of railways and of modern development, it is rather a pity and rather a reflection on our consideration for the earlier parts of Canada that they are yet without those railway facilities for which I am craving the attention of the Government to-night. There is no good reason at all why a county like the county of Victoria, which I am representing here, and in reference to which I am particularly urging this railway, should not have the great boon of railway connection with the outside world.
It might be asked if we have any particularly important industries in that part of the country. I find that we have in the small province of Nova Scotia a great many industries, large exports and large developments, and th(it in the island of Cape Breton we have no doubt the largest of those developments. I wish to point out very briefly from a calculation made about the yearly production of wealth in the province of Nova Scotia that in coal we produced last year $22,500,000; in coke, $2,600,000; in gold and other minerals, $125,000; in gypsum, limestone, etc., $800,000; in building materials, $410,000; in pigiron, $2,500,000; in steel, steel rails and rods, $17,550,000 ; in fisheries, $8,000,000 in manufactures, ships and freight, $46,250,000; in the products of
the farm, $31,100,000; in the products of the forest, $5,000,000; in game and furs, $500,000. For the small province of Nova Scotia with a population of only about 500,000 or 600,000, I submit that the record is very creditable and that, when we are asking that something should be done for us in the way of further railway extension, we are only asking what we think the importance of the province demands, and particularly the importance of that section which now has no railway facilities at all.
It is a policy expatiated upon >by my hon. friends opposite that we should not by any aet'of our own permit our raw material to go out of the country, if it is going out of the country to our disadvantage. I submit that there is no better or more important raw material within the confines of our Dominion than our fisheries. Fish may be considered a raw material; it is not of course manufactured to any great extent, but it is a material, a product, a property of this country which is exceedingly important, and in the provinces of Nova Scotia and- New Brunswick our fisheries are one of the greatest assets we have, as witness in this statement that the fisheries in the province of Nova Scotia last year were $8,000,000, and this produced under great disadvantages. For the transportation of fish we have practically no facilities whatever. One of the best sections for fisheries is along the coast of the county of Victoria, which I have the honour to represent, and in which we have practically no railway facilities at all. The reason I say that this raw material goes out of the Dominion of Canada, because we are not able to handle it ourselves, is that American fishermen in large numbers visit the coast of the island of Cape Breton, of the county of Victoria, anchor off our coast, load up with our fish and go away to the United States. The fish is then put under some process and kept in the United States until they can take advantage of our markets in Ottawa, Montreal, Winnipeg and other Canadian cities. The fish comes back to us; we pay duty on it and pay much higher prices than we would have to pay if we kept that fish in the first instance in our own province and under our own control.
I submit that it is impossible to keep these American vessels from fishing inside the three-mile limit, and it is impossible to keep them from taking away our fish when we have not proper facilities to deal with it ourselves. If we had the extension of the Intercolonial railway through the

island of Cape Breton along these fishing places, both on the south of the island and on the north and along the coast of the county of Victoria, we should be in a position at all seasons to reach our own markets and prevent the necessity of our people dealing entirely with a foreign country, and prevent this excellent food which is so much needed and would be so much appreciated by our own people, from going out of our own country. At present, it is impossible for our people generally to take advantage of it, because the transportation to the United States, the handling of it there, the bringing of it back again and paying the duty, puts it at such a price that the ordinary man is not able to take advantage of it. If this railway were built through the county of Victoria down to Bay St. Lawrence, touching at the different fishing stations along that coast, with proper cold-storage along the line and also in the city of Montreal, which is the western terminus of the Intercolonial railway, we should be able without difficulty to place this magnificent fish, fresh out of the water, at the disposal of the people of our own country. And this is only one of the industries the resources for which are to be found in that part of the country. We have a good lumbering country, we have vast quantities of gypsum, and we have incalculable quantities of limestone along these hills, which is in great demand at the steel works at Sydney and North Sydney, which markets at present it cannot reach. These resources also could be developed if we had this railway.
The whole length of the road of which I speak would be about 125 miles. We had 22 miles of that road practically under contract before the change in Government took place. Reference to the speeches of the Minister of Railways last year will show that $22,000 was voted in 1911 to make a start on the road. Some money was voted to start in tire county of Guys-borough under the same conditions and the same provisions made by the late Government for a railway started between Dartmouth and Dean, in the county of Halifax. That is under construction. It was the scheme of the Government of that day to carry all these lines along at the same time. I have repeatedly brought to the notice of the Prime Minister and the Government the fact that they dropped the Victoria end of this proposition and went on with the Halifax end. I cannot go into that to-night. The Government know

the attitude that I have taken; they know that I have complained, somewhat bitterly, that all the lines under construction by the late Government and provided for by them were not treated alike, but that different treatment has been meted out to the county of Victoria from that of the county of Halifax. The great necessity of building this road in the county' of Victoria has been again and again pressed upon the attention of the Government, and I am sure that the Prime Minister, himself a Nova Scotian and who knows the county of which I am talking, realizes the importance of dealing with this question. As I have said, I regret that the Minister of Railways is not in his place. I served notice on the acting Minister of Railways that this resolution was to be moved, and I hope he will be able to give us some idea of what the prospects are of this being taken up by the Government and carried out at an early date. The good people of the county of Victoria have been contributing their part to the building of railways in this country for the sixty years, or whatever the time may be, since the Government of Nova Scotia and the Government of the Dominion undertook the building of railways as a Government business. We have never found fault with the development of other parts of the country. But I am sure you will admit, Mr. Speaker, that now, after about 150 years of settlement, in that old part of this great country, that a settlement, with the products they already have to send to market and the developments that they have a right to look for, shall be obliged to send for 150 miles to a railway without the Government immediately attempting to take away the disability under which they have suffered for so many years. I trust the Government will at an early day revive the interest that was taken in 1911 in this railway extension into the county of Victoria, and will re-vote that money and start in anew for the development of that railway-not only the few miles in contemplation then but the extension throughout the length of the county of Victoria to these fishing villages and other places capable of yielding traffic to which I have referred. So far as the fishing villages are concerned, we shall never deal properly with this great industry of fishing until we have a line of railways not only in Victoria, but through the counties of Inverness, Richmond and Cape Breton, where there are the same facilities for the fishing industry, and where railway facilities are equally required.

I regret that the hon.
member has not seen fit to ask for an extension of the Intercolonial railway into the non-railway sections of the .province of Quebec as well as into those of the Maritime provinces.

I mentioned in my
speech the province of Quebec, and we in Hova Scotia regard Quebec as a Maritime province, as I maintained in my address.

I am glad to accept the hon. gentleman's statement. But as the resolution reads it does not cover that .point. There is a peculiar case regarding the county I have the honour to represent in this House, so far as the extension of the Intercolonial railway in the province of Quebec is concerned. The Intercolonial railway from Levis to Montreal is the old Drummond County railway. At the time the Drummond County railway was purchased, I complained in my county, as did all the counties of the south shore of the Sti Lawrence from Levis to Montreal, that the Intercolonial railway was not built along the .south shore. It is a good section of the country, a good farming district, and of course the present route of the Intercolonial railway from Montreal to Levis was then served by the Drummond County railway, which had been subsidized by the federal and local governments and all the municipalities. There was a branch of the Drummond County line starting from St. Leonard junction running to the shores of lake St. Peter, to the town of Nicolefc. The Drummond County railway had to be completely rebuilt by the Intercolonial railway. It was an old road which had been used for lumber purposes by the company which had control of it, and now again the road has to be practically rebuilt from St. Leonard junction up to Nicolet. I would submit that when this .Government decide to make extensions of the Intercolonial railway, instead of .starting from St. Leonard and running to Nicolet, they should run from Drummondville to Nicolet, going through the parishes of St. Joachim de Courval, St. Zephyrin de Courval, La Visitation and Ste. Monique de Nicolet. At present the road runs from St. Leonard through Ste. Monique to Nicolet. If it started from Drummondville, going through the parishes I have mentioned into Nicolet, it would be quite an important change, and that part of the railroad would be put on a paying basis, although it is not at present paying. It is
absolutely plain building; no bridges would be required, and the Intercolonial railway could start at Drummondville, from the east side of the St. Francis river, going to the north side of the Nicolet river. There would be no bridges, and I really think that the municipalities of St. Joachim, St. Zephyrin, La Visitation and Ste. Monique	would help, by	giving
rights of way or perhaps subsidies, to rebuild that section of the Intercolonial railway. The town of Drummondville is a very important point. It connects with the Canadian Pacific railway going to the United States and with the Intercolonial railway going to St. Hyacinthe. St. Leonard junction is not an important point on the Intercolonial railway, but it was used in former times by the Drummond County railway as a shipping point for St. Lawrence traffic. A petition will be placed before the Minister of Railways by the population of those parishes, which comprise a very important farming district. I thought this was a convenient time to express my opinion as far as the electors of my county have expressed it to me. The Intercolonial railway now coming to Montreal should make every effort possible to help the south shore of the St. Lawrence. It has been deprived of very important railway facilities. The Quebec, Montreal and Southern railway, which starts at St. Lambert and goes, to Fortier-ville, is a very poor railroad. It gives the poorest service in the province of Quebec. The Intercolonial railway is about twenty-five miles from the shore of the St. Lawrence. I would advise that if the Government is making extensions it should serve the parishes I have just mentioned, so that the line, instead of running from St. Leonard to Nicolet, would run from Drummondville to Nicolet. Undoubtedly it would then be on a paying basis and help considerably that part of the county of Yam-aska, a certain part of the county of Nico-let, and a certain part of Drummond county. That proposition would have the support of the boards of trade of Drummond and Nicolet. However, I shall not go into the details at this late hour. I hope that when the Government decide to extend the Intercolonial railway _ in the Maritime provinces, in the sections of country which are not now served by railways, they will do the same to the province of Quebec, and especially improve, in all possible ways, the branches of the Intercolonial railway that it now has in that province.

Oil account of the lateness of the hour and the failure of the minister to bring down the report for which I asked a year ago, I shall not address the House to-night. I would ask if there is any reason why I cannot have this report for which I moved a year ago. I may say that I received from the minister permission to read the report and have done so. It is very favourable to the construction of the road I propose to speak on, but there are certain facts contained in it which I would like to place on ' Hansard.'

I inquired in the
department about this report. I find that it has been prepared and it would have been placed on the table to-day were it not that it has to go to the Secretary of State's Department. It will be laid on the table to-morrow or the next day. The hon. member will have an opportunity of taking up this subject on the Estimates, when the Intercolonial railway .is under discussion.

In answer t>t my hon. friend from Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie), I acknowledge with appreciation his kindly reference to my friend the Minister of Railways (.Mr. Cochrane), and I am sure my hon. friend will be pleased to know, as will all other members of the House, that my hon. friend the acting Minister of Railways had a cablegram today which goes to show that the Minister of Railways is making very marked improvement as a result of his trip and the rest he is having since he left here.
I regret that the Prime Minister is not in his seat this evening, as, in my humble judgment, the matter which has been brought to the attention of the House in respect not alone to Nova Scotia but to Quebec, in connection with the extensions of the branch lines of the Intercolonial railway to these various portions of the provinces where such extensions are required, is one of serious moment and one of such importance that undoubtedly it will receive the special consideration of the Prime Minister, as I am sure it will of the acting Minister of Railways and Canals. We all agree with what has been said. I was struck by the figures which the hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) gave in regard to production in the province of Nova Scotia. Those figures give evidence of the great natural resources of that province, and the same applies to the province of Quebec and to the other provinces directly interested in this matter. I will

take an early opportunity of drawing the attention of the Prime Minister to the statements which have been made this evening with respect to this matter. As my hon. friend the member for Cape Breton well knows, the Prime Minister is very deeply interested in everything that will promote the welfare and development not only of the Maritime provinces but of all the provinces of the Dominion.
